Embodied First Exam — dexterous tasks on the Tianji + Wuji 2 rig

The Embodied First Exam labels 62 of its 1,156 tasks as dexterous-hand tasks. This page covers the 51 of them in its two suites DexHandExam and DexToolBench (code, MIT). Both suites already run on MuJoCo, the engine our tracking policy is deployed in, so a scene is ported by taking the model the original code builds, with its geometry, masses, contact parameters, materials, lights and cameras unchanged, and replacing only the robot by ours: two Tianji M6 arms with Wuji 2 hands.

How to read the status. Every statement on a card comes from a recorded step. Original scene exported: the model built by the original code is saved with its assets. Dynamics compared with the original: the same recorded actions were replayed in the original environment and in our MuJoCo with the original robot still in place, and the two state histories were compared; the numbers are on the card. Our robot in the scene: the original robot was removed and our rig put in; the scene's own bodies and contact parameters were checked to be unchanged. A card without these lines has only its description recorded. Nothing here says that a task has been solved.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Assemble a neatly aligned hamburger

Assemble a neat hamburger on the serving plate. The bottom bun already rests on the plate; the beef patty, cheese slice, tomato slice, lettuce leaf and top bun start separately on preparation supports. Stack them from bottom to top in exactly this order: bottom bun, patty, cheese, tomato, lettuce, top bun. Success requires all six layers at the same time: every ingredient center within 12 mm horizontally of the plate center, every layer upright within 0.22 radians, heights strictly increasing in recipe order, all five consecutive pairs in physical contact and the bottom bun touching the plate. Then release the hamburger: with no hand contact on any ingredient, every ingredient linear speed at most 0.025 m/s and angular speed at most 0.25 rad/s, the complete condition must hold for 100 consecutive controls (2 s). The episode ends with success at that moment; a partial stack never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when any ingredient touches the table top or the floor (dropped, or knocked off its support, the plate or the stack), when any ingredient body falls below the table top (z < 0.30 m) or leaves the workspace box x in [-0.64, 0.64] m, y in [-0.52, 0.52] m, z in [0.30, 0.80] m, when a passive cheese or lettuce bending angle exceeds 0.65 radians, or when the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; no object teleports, grasp welds, scripted object motion or direct ingredient forces. Lettuce and cheese use three passive elastic strips; other ingredients are rigid contact proxies. This task evaluates assembly under that approximation, not continuum food deformation or ingredient damage. The episode allows at most 7500 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

You control one dexterous hand mounted on a six-DoF wrist positioning stage (three prismatic and three serial revolute
joints, no arm). The stage and the fingers are position actuated in the physics engine under native force bounds;
grasping, carrying and releasing require physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics
substeps.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Both hands hang from the same six-axis wrist stage, with the same wrist joints, ranges, gains and start targets.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`28` for `sharpa`, `26` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).
Full task description (original text, privileged setting; differs from the standard one)
# DexHand: Assemble a neatly aligned hamburger

Assemble a neat hamburger on the serving plate. The bottom bun already rests on the plate; the beef patty, cheese slice, tomato slice, lettuce leaf and top bun start separately on preparation supports. Stack them from bottom to top in exactly this order: bottom bun, patty, cheese, tomato, lettuce, top bun. Success requires all six layers at the same time: every ingredient center within 12 mm horizontally of the plate center, every layer upright within 0.22 radians, heights strictly increasing in recipe order, all five consecutive pairs in physical contact and the bottom bun touching the plate. Then release the hamburger: with no hand contact on any ingredient, every ingredient linear speed at most 0.025 m/s and angular speed at most 0.25 rad/s, the complete condition must hold for 100 consecutive controls (2 s). The episode ends with success at that moment; a partial stack never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when any ingredient touches the table top or the floor (dropped, or knocked off its support, the plate or the stack), when any ingredient body falls below the table top (z < 0.30 m) or leaves the workspace box x in [-0.64, 0.64] m, y in [-0.52, 0.52] m, z in [0.30, 0.80] m, when a passive cheese or lettuce bending angle exceeds 0.65 radians, or when the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; no object teleports, grasp welds, scripted object motion or direct ingredient forces. Lettuce and cheese use three passive elastic strips; other ingredients are rigid contact proxies. This task evaluates assembly under that approximation, not continuum food deformation or ingredient damage. The episode allows at most 7500 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

You control one dexterous hand mounted on a six-DoF wrist positioning stage (three prismatic and three serial revolute
joints, no arm). The stage and the fingers are position actuated in the physics engine under native force bounds;
grasping, carrying and releasing require physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics
substeps.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Both hands hang from the same six-axis wrist stage, with the same wrist joints, ranges, gains and start targets.
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `28` wide for `sharpa` and `26` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control. The first six entries are the wrist-stage targets, identical for both hands:
`wrist_x, wrist_y, wrist_z` (metres, world frame) and `wrist_rx, wrist_ry, wrist_rz` (radians, serial XYZ joints, not a
quaternion). The finger targets follow in native actuator order, in radians:

- `sharpa`: 28 values, the six wrist targets and 22 Sharpa Wave finger targets `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `right_pinky_DIP`.
- `wuji`: 26 values, the same six wrist targets and 20 Wuji Hand 2.2 finger targets `r_wuji_r_THJ0..3`,
  `r_wuji_r_FFJ0..3`, `r_wuji_r_MFJ0..3`, `r_wuji_r_RFJ0..3`, `r_wuji_r_LFJ0..3`.

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`. Both hands start from the same wrist targets; the frozen
finger start pose of each hand is in `task.json` (`initial_targets`).

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 28)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 26)`
for `wuji`, at most 7500 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

DexHand: Whisk batter in a bowl, drain and set the whisk down

dexhand-batter-whisk-i00 · upstream folder tasks/dexhand/dexhand-batter-whisk-i00-standard
our robot in the scenecore setoriginal robot: marvin-bimanual-sharpa-wavedifficulty: hardupstream status: provisionaloriginal hands: sharpa, wuji50 Hz controlat most 4000 controls5 stages
Pick a balloon whisk up off the rim of a steel bowl with a dexterous hand on a Tianji Marvin arm (Sharpa Wave by default, or Wuji Hand 2.2; the second arm and hand may steady the bowl), whisk the batter with at least five revolutions, lift the whisk out to drain over the bowl and lay it down on the counter; the bowl must not tip or slide.
  • Original environment (the task's own code in its Docker image, MuJoCo 3.4.0), packaged reference actions, control rows counted from 0: Sharpa Wave: success after 1,816 controls (stages reached at control rows 536, 923, 1359, 1427 and 1815). The start-state hash equals the one frozen in the task, in MuJoCo 3.4.0 and in 3.8.0. The scene text built on our machine equals the one built in the image.
  • Same engine (the original's own engine, MuJoCo 3.4.0): the exported scene file, stepped by the port's own loop, gives exactly the bits of the original code: the full simulation state after every one of 7,886 controls, over the reference and 5 perturbed copies of it, for Sharpa Wave.
  • Same engine (our engine, MuJoCo 3.8.0): the exported scene file, stepped by the port's own loop, gives exactly the bits of the original code: the full simulation state after every one of 2,826 controls, over the reference and 5 perturbed copies of it, for Sharpa Wave.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Whisk batter in a bowl, drain and set the whisk down

Pick up the balloon whisk, whisk the batter in the steel bowl, drain the whisk over the bowl and lay it down on the counter. The whisk starts at rest, leaning on the bowl rim with its handle end on the counter (where it settles when released from the source scene's start pose, standing in the bowl); both hands start open. The batter is not simulated: whisking is measured on the whisk-head point, 20 mm above the wire tip on the whisk axis, which is in the batter while it is between 3 mm above the bowl origin and the batter surface (35.7 mm above the bowl origin) and at least 4 mm inside the bowl wall. Complete five stages in order. (1) Picked up: a hand holds the whisk clear of everything else, i.e. the robot touches it, it touches neither the counter nor the bowl and its lowest point is at least 30 mm above the counter top, for 10 consecutive controls. (2) Immersed: the head point enters the batter. (3) Whisked: the head point circles the bowl axis by at least 5 full revolutions of net (signed, unwrapped) angle while it stays in the batter; leaving the batter before 5 revolutions resets the count to zero, and controls with the head point closer than 8 mm to the bowl axis add nothing. (4) Drained: while the robot touches the whisk, the wire tip is at least 10 mm above the bowl rim, the head point is within 55 mm of the bowl axis (over the opening) and the whisk hangs head-down within 30 degrees of vertical, for 25 consecutive controls (0.5 s). (5) Set down: lower the whisk until it touches the counter top while the robot still touches it (it is then placed), then let go; the episode succeeds when, for 50 consecutive controls (1 s), the whisk touches the counter top, touches neither the robot nor the bowl, lies within 30 degrees of horizontal with its centre of mass at least 120 mm from the bowl axis, and its centre of mass moves slower than 0.02 m/s and it turns slower than 0.3 rad/s. The episode ends with success at that moment; partial completion never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every control, when: the bowl tilts more than 10 degrees, slides more than 30 mm or rises more than 20 mm from its start; after the pickup, the whisk touches nothing, its lowest point is more than 2 mm above the counter top and its centre of mass moves downward faster than 0.2 m/s (dropped); after the pickup and before it is placed, the whisk touches the counter or is out of robot contact for more than 10 consecutive controls (dropped); after it is placed, the whisk touches neither the robot nor the counter for more than 5 consecutive controls (tossed); the bowl or the whisk touches the floor, has its centre of mass below the counter top (z < 0.68 m) or outside the workspace x in [0.25, 0.99] m, y in [-0.36, 0.36] m, z in [0.60, 1.50] m; or the physics becomes unstable. Before the pickup the whisk may be nudged or slide off the rim; the counter, floor and workspace rules still apply. Later actions cannot undo a failure. "Robot" means any hand, arm link or the stand. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; no object teleports, grasp welds, scripted object motion or direct forces. The episode allows at most 4000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

The robot is a fixed Tianji Marvin stand at the world origin facing +x, with two 7-joint arms and a dexterous hand
on each wrist (robot id `marvin-bimanual-sharpa-wave`). Every arm and finger joint is a position servo in the physics
engine under native force bounds; arm servos have stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad and **no gravity
compensation** (a held target sags by about 1 cm at the hand under load unless your targets account for it). The bowl
and the whisk move only through contact with the hands, the arms, each other and the counter. The controller runs at
50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps. World frame: metres and radians, +z up, +x forward from the robot stand, +y to
the robot's left.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`). The right arm/hand picks up and uses the whisk; the left arm/hand may steady the bowl.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`58` for `sharpa`, `54` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

Complete five stages in order. (1) Picked up: a hand holds the whisk clear of everything else, i.e. the robot touches it, it touches neither the counter nor the bowl and its lowest point is at least 30 mm above the counter top, for 10 consecutive controls. (2) Immersed: the head point enters the batter. (3) Whisked: the head point circles the bowl axis by at least 5 full revolutions of net (signed, unwrapped) angle while it stays in the batter; leaving the batter before 5 revolutions resets the count to zero, and controls with the head point closer than 8 mm to the bowl axis add nothing. (4) Drained: while the robot touches the whisk, the wire tip is at least 10 mm above the bowl rim, the head point is within 55 mm of the bowl axis (over the opening) and the whisk hangs head-down within 30 degrees of vertical, for 25 consecutive controls (0.5 s). (5) Set down: lower the whisk until it touches the counter top while the robot still touches it (it is then placed), then let go; the episode succeeds when, for 50 consecutive controls (1 s), the whisk touches the counter top, touches neither the robot nor the bowl, lies within 30 degrees of horizontal with its centre of mass at least 120 mm from the bowl axis, and its centre of mass moves slower than 0.02 m/s and it turns slower than 0.3 rad/s. The episode ends with success at that moment; partial completion never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every control, when: the bowl tilts more than 10 degrees, slides more than 30 mm or rises more than 20 mm from its start; after the pickup, the whisk touches nothing, its lowest point is more than 2 mm above the counter top and its centre of mass moves downward faster than 0.2 m/s (dropped); after the pickup and before it is placed, the whisk touches the counter or is out of robot contact for more than 10 consecutive controls (dropped); after it is placed, the whisk touches neither the robot nor the counter for more than 5 consecutive controls (tossed); the bowl or the whisk touches the floor, has its centre of mass below the counter top (z < 0.68 m) or outside the workspace x in [0.25, 0.99] m, y in [-0.36, 0.36] m, z in [0.60, 1.50] m; or the physics becomes unstable. Before the pickup the whisk may be nudged or slide off the rim; the counter, floor and workspace rules still apply. Later actions cannot undo a failure. "Robot" means any hand, arm link or the stand. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; no object teleports, grasp welds, scripted object motion or direct forces. The episode allows at most 4000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

The robot is a fixed Tianji Marvin stand at the world origin facing +x, with two 7-joint arms and a dexterous hand
on each wrist (robot id `marvin-bimanual-sharpa-wave`). Every arm and finger joint is a position servo in the physics
engine under native force bounds; arm servos have stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad and **no gravity
compensation** (a held target sags by about 1 cm at the hand under load unless your targets account for it). The bowl
and the whisk move only through contact with the hands, the arms, each other and the counter. The controller runs at
50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps. World frame: metres and radians, +z up, +x forward from the robot stand, +y to
the robot's left.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`). The right arm/hand picks up and uses the whisk; the left arm/hand may steady the bowl.
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `58` wide for `sharpa` and `54` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control with a position target for every actuator, in model order (`s.actuator_names`):

- columns 0-6: left arm `SHOULDER_PITCH_L_J1, SHOULDER_ROLL_L_J2, ELBOW_PITCH_L_J3, ELBOW_YAW_L_J4, WRIST_PITCH_L_J5,
  WRIST_YAW_L_J6, WRIST_ROLL_L_J7` (each name + `_target`); columns 7-13: the right arm `..._R_J1` to `..._R_J7`;
- `sharpa` (58 values): columns 14-35 the left Sharpa Wave fingers `left_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `left_pinky_DIP`, columns
  36-57 the right Sharpa Wave fingers `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `right_pinky_DIP`;
- `wuji` (54 values): columns 14-33 the left Wuji Hand 2.2 fingers (`l_wuji_*`, vendor order), columns 34-53 the
  right Wuji fingers (`r_wuji_*`).

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`. Both hands start open above the counter with the arms in a
ready pose (`task.json` `reset_state[<hand>]`: joint positions and start targets); `s.hold_action()` at reset keeps
that pose. The whisk does not start in a hand: it rests against the bowl rim with its handle end on the counter, where
it settles when released from the source scene's start pose (standing in the bowl). The left hand may steady the bowl
(for example while the right hand lifts the whisk off its rim); the success predicate does not require it.

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 58)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 54)`
for `wuji`, at most 4000 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Inflate a tire with a portable bicycle pump

Inflate the bicycle tire with the portable bicycle pump, using the right hand of the Tianji Marvin robot that stands at the bench (stand at the world origin, facing +x; the left arm stays parked). A mini floor pump (Topeak Mini Morph type, 154 g class, barrel 0.25 m tall) stands free on its folding foot on the bench next to a 406 (20 inch) wheel lying on the bench; as in the source scene, the pump's hose head starts disconnected from the wheel's Schrader valve and the tire is at 200.0 kPa gauge. The head (TRK-RP04 type) sits on the valve stem's axis 17.5 mm out from its seat (an 8 mm gap to the stem tip) with its thumb lock open (lever pointing up). The head moves only along the stem axis: a passive slide guided by the hose, with 2 N of friction and an end stop at the seat; pushing it 17.5 mm toward the rim seats it on the stem. The thumb lock is a passive hinge on the head (axis along world y, at the lever's foot, 0.004 N m friction) that turns 1.65 rad from up (open) to lying flat toward the wheel hub (closed). The pump's T handle rests at the top of its 0.20 m travel: the piston is a passive slide whose compressed-air spring pushes the handle back up (about 6 N at the top and 46 N at the bottom of the stroke) with viscous damping and 1 N seal friction. A stroke counts only while the head is connected (see stage 1), when the handle is pushed down to a piston depth of at least 0.18 m (90 % of the travel) and then returns to a depth of at most 0.04 m (20 %); shallower strokes never count and are not failures. The tire pressure is a checker quantity, not simulated air: every counted stroke adds 380 Pa (the mean rise per stroke of the source gas model, which reaches 210.6 kPa after its 28 strokes). Success requires, in this order: (1) the head connected: seated within 0.5 mm of its 17.5 mm travel while the thumb lock is closed to within 0.15 rad of its 1.65 rad stop (this latches; a stroke is armed and counted only while the head is seated and locked like this at that very moment); (2) at least 28 counted strokes; (3) tire pressure at least 210.6 kPa gauge; (4) the head disconnected again, as at the end of the source: the thumb lock opened to at most 0.5 rad and the head pulled at least 12.5 mm back off its seat (off the 9.5 mm stem engagement; this latches; the pressure stays, since only counted strokes change it); (5) the handle released at the top: piston depth at most 0.01 m, no contact of any robot part (hands, arms, stand) with any part of the pump or the head, pump tilt at most 0.0873 rad (5 degrees) from upright, pump centre-of-mass speed at most 0.02 m/s and handle speed at most 0.02 m/s, held continuously for 50 consecutive controls (1 s). The episode ends with success at that moment. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when the pump tilts more than 0.2618 rad (15 degrees) from upright, when its base moves more than 0.03 m horizontally from its start or rises more than 0.02 m above it, when its centre of mass falls below the bench top (z < 0.70 m) or any pump part touches the floor, when the head, once connected and before stage 3 is reached, is pulled back more than 2 mm from its seat or its thumb lock is opened below 1.2 rad (head_disconnected), when the head is pulled back more than 2 mm from its seat while its thumb lock is still closed (at least 1.2 rad) after stage 3 (head_forced_off: open the lock first), or when the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. The episode allows at most 5000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed (the Marvin arm joints and the hands' finger joints); no object teleports, grasp welds, scripted object motion or direct object forces. The wheel, valve and hose are static props (the hose end at the head moves with the head, for display only); the head and its thumb lock move only through contact.

You control the right arm and right hand of a fixed Tianji Marvin robot: a stand with two 7-joint arms and a dexterous
hand on each wrist, standing at the bench with its base centre at the world origin, facing +x (shoulders at z = 1.121 m,
1.221 m above the floor). The left arm stays parked beside the torso with its hand open; the task is done by the right arm and hand
alone. Every arm and finger joint is a position servo inside the physics engine under native force bounds; arm servos
have stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad and **no gravity compensation** (a held target sags under the arm's
weight and the handle's push unless your targets account for it). Pushing the pump handle requires physical contact.
The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`); the left arm is parked and only the right arm/hand perform the task.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`58` for `sharpa`, `54` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

## What you observe
Camera RGB and calibrated depth from `overview` (default) and `closeup` (aimed at the pump), the robot's own joint
positions, velocities, actuator efforts, hand pose and current targets, and robot-link forward kinematics. The
service does not report the pump pose, the head or lever position, the piston depth, the stroke count, the tire
pressure or contacts: judge the
handle and the pump from the images and depth. At the end of an episode the meta reports `done`, `success` and a
failure category; that is the graded verdict (see the task text).

You control the right arm and right hand of a fixed Tianji Marvin robot: a stand with two 7-joint arms and a dexterous
hand on each wrist, standing at the bench with its base centre at the world origin, facing +x (shoulders at z = 1.121 m,
1.221 m above the floor). The left arm stays parked beside the torso with its hand open; the task is done by the right arm and hand
alone. Every arm and finger joint is a position servo inside the physics engine under native force bounds; arm servos
have stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad and **no gravity compensation** (a held target sags under the arm's
weight and the handle's push unless your targets account for it). Pushing the pump handle requires physical contact.
The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`); the left arm is parked and only the right arm/hand perform the task.
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `58` wide for `sharpa` and `54` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control and holds a position target for every actuator, in radians:

- `sharpa` (58 values): 0-6 the left arm `SHOULDER_PITCH_L_J1, SHOULDER_ROLL_L_J2, ELBOW_PITCH_L_J3, ELBOW_YAW_L_J4,
  WRIST_PITCH_L_J5, WRIST_YAW_L_J6, WRIST_ROLL_L_J7` (actuators `<joint>_target`; keep them at the parked start
  values), 7-13 the same right-arm joints (`..._R_J1` to `..._R_J7`), 14-35 the 22 left Sharpa Wave finger targets
  `left_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `left_pinky_DIP`, 36-57 the 22 right Sharpa Wave finger targets `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ...
  `right_pinky_DIP`.
- `wuji` (54 values): 0-13 the same arm targets, 14-33 the 20 left Wuji Hand 2.2 finger targets `l_wuji_l_THJ0..3`,
  `l_wuji_l_FFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_MFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_RFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_LFJ0..3`, 34-53 the 20 right ones
  (`r_wuji_r_...`, same order).

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`. The frozen start targets of each hand are in `task.json`
(`initial_targets`): the right hand starts open, palm down, above and to the right of the pump. The right hand's frame
is the body `wrist_stage` on the right flange (fingers along its +z, palm normal +x, thumb +y), which forward
kinematics of the arm joints places in the world.

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 58)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 54)`
for `wuji`, at most 5000 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

DexHand: Load two punched pages into a ring binder

dexhand-binder-page-load-i00 · upstream folder tasks/dexhand/dexhand-binder-page-load-i00-standard

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Load two punched pages into a ring binder

Load both punched pages into the open-front ring binder on the desk. The binder (free on the desk, back cover towards +x) has three 1-inch round split rings on two toggle plates with an over-centre spring: both plates rest closed at 0 rad and open at 0.60 rad, and a booster paddle at each end of the mechanism opens them when pressed down. Two rigid punched pages (139.7 x 215.9 mm, 6 g, three 6.35 mm holes 9.5 mm from the binding edge) lie loose and flat on the desk, printed face up, holes towards the binder (-x), as in the source scene. Complete these stages in order. (1) Rings opened: both toggle plates at 0.50 rad or more. (2) Pages placed: with the rings still open (0.50 rad or more), every one of the six holes is threaded by the right ring half of its own station (the ring wire centre line crosses the page plane exactly once within 3.5 mm of the hole centre, the left half not at all), no hand contact on either page, each page touches the binder or the other page, and each page centre (60 mm from the hole line into the sheet) lies over the back cover: binder-frame x in (0.03, 0.16) m, |y| < 0.03 m, z in (-0.01, 0.06) m. (3) Rings closed: both toggle plates at 0.05 rad or less, every hole linked exactly once by its closed ring (one crossing within 3.5 mm of the hole centre) and both page centres over the back cover. (4) Release: the stage-3 condition with no hand contact on any page or any binder part, both pages resting on the binder and each page staying within 2 mm and 0.03 rad of its pose at the start of the window, for 50 consecutive controls (1 s). The episode ends with success at that moment; one page, an unthreaded hole or open rings never count. The episode ends at once with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when a page touches the floor; when a page has no contact at all, falls faster than 0.2 m/s and no ring runs through any of its holes (dropped); when a page origin goes more than 2 mm below the desk top (z < 0.698 m) or leaves the workspace x in [0.20, 0.98] m, y in [-0.38, 0.48] m, z in [0.698, 1.10] m; when the binder moves more than 0.03 m horizontally from its start or tilts more than 0.35 rad; when a ring wire penetrates a page deeper than 1.2 mm or a hand part penetrates a page deeper than 3 mm (a ring can only enter a page through its hole); or when the physics becomes unstable. Later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; the rings, plates, boosters and covers move only through contact and their passive joints. Pages may slide on the desk and hang over its edge (a page touching the desk is not a failure). Pages are stiff cardstock plates: paper bending is not modelled. At most 6000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

You control one dexterous hand mounted on a six-DoF wrist positioning stage (three prismatic and three serial revolute
joints, no arm). The stage and the fingers are position actuated in the physics engine under native force bounds;
grasping, carrying and releasing require physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics
substeps.

## Scene and modelling notes
The binder is free on the desk: back cover (with the ring mechanism near its spine edge) towards +x, spine and front
cover on passive hinges towards -x. Its two toggle plates carry the three ring halves on each side; an over-centre
housing spring (a passive spatial tendon) holds them either closed (0 rad) or open (0.60 rad), and the plates and the
two booster paddles are coupled by the binder's internal linkage (passive joint couplings, never attached to the hand).
Pressing a booster paddle down opens the rings; pushing the plates back past the over-centre point (for example by
pressing the raised inner edges of the open plates down) closes them.
Simplifications, stated plainly: the pages are rigid 0.8 mm cardstock plates (paper bending, creasing and tearing are
not modelled; the holes are octagonal openings 6.35 mm across flats); as in the source scene the two sheets start loose and
flat on the desk (a hand can drag a page so that its far edge overhangs the desk edge, then pinch it); the binder geometry is
an authored reconstruction (Avery 05806 dimensions), not manufacturer CAD.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Both hands hang from the same six-axis wrist stage, with the same wrist joints, ranges, gains and start targets.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`28` for `sharpa`, `26` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

(3) Rings closed: both toggle plates at 0.05 rad or less, every hole linked exactly once by its closed ring (one crossing within 3.5 mm of the hole centre) and both page centres over the back cover. (4) Release: the stage-3 condition with no hand contact on any page or any binder part, both pages resting on the binder and each page staying within 2 mm and 0.03 rad of its pose at the start of the window, for 50 consecutive controls (1 s). The episode ends with success at that moment; one page, an unthreaded hole or open rings never count. The episode ends at once with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when a page touches the floor; when a page has no contact at all, falls faster than 0.2 m/s and no ring runs through any of its holes (dropped); when a page origin goes more than 2 mm below the desk top (z < 0.698 m) or leaves the workspace x in [0.20, 0.98] m, y in [-0.38, 0.48] m, z in [0.698, 1.10] m; when the binder moves more than 0.03 m horizontally from its start or tilts more than 0.35 rad; when a ring wire penetrates a page deeper than 1.2 mm or a hand part penetrates a page deeper than 3 mm (a ring can only enter a page through its hole); or when the physics becomes unstable. Later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; the rings, plates, boosters and covers move only through contact and their passive joints. Pages may slide on the desk and hang over its edge (a page touching the desk is not a failure). Pages are stiff cardstock plates: paper bending is not modelled. At most 6000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

You control one dexterous hand mounted on a six-DoF wrist positioning stage (three prismatic and three serial revolute
joints, no arm). The stage and the fingers are position actuated in the physics engine under native force bounds;
grasping, carrying and releasing require physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics
substeps.

## Scene and modelling notes
The binder is free on the desk: back cover (with the ring mechanism near its spine edge) towards +x, spine and front
cover on passive hinges towards -x. Its two toggle plates carry the three ring halves on each side; an over-centre
housing spring (a passive spatial tendon) holds them either closed (0 rad) or open (0.60 rad), and the plates and the
two booster paddles are coupled by the binder's internal linkage (passive joint couplings, never attached to the hand).
Pressing a booster paddle down opens the rings; pushing the plates back past the over-centre point (for example by
pressing the raised inner edges of the open plates down) closes them.
Simplifications, stated plainly: the pages are rigid 0.8 mm cardstock plates (paper bending, creasing and tearing are
not modelled; the holes are octagonal openings 6.35 mm across flats); as in the source scene the two sheets start loose and
flat on the desk (a hand can drag a page so that its far edge overhangs the desk edge, then pinch it); the binder geometry is
an authored reconstruction (Avery 05806 dimensions), not manufacturer CAD.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Both hands hang from the same six-axis wrist stage, with the same wrist joints, ranges, gains and start targets.
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `28` wide for `sharpa` and `26` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control. The first six entries are the wrist-stage targets, identical for both hands:
`wrist_x, wrist_y, wrist_z` (metres, world-aligned offsets from `wrist_base`) and `wrist_rx, wrist_ry, wrist_rz` (radians, serial XYZ joints, not a
quaternion). The finger targets follow in native actuator order, in radians:

- `sharpa`: 28 values, the six wrist targets and 22 Sharpa Wave finger targets `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `right_pinky_DIP`.
- `wuji`: 26 values, the same six wrist targets and 20 Wuji Hand 2.2 finger targets `r_wuji_r_THJ0..3`,
  `r_wuji_r_FFJ0..3`, `r_wuji_r_MFJ0..3`, `r_wuji_r_RFJ0..3`, `r_wuji_r_LFJ0..3`.

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`. Both hands start from the same wrist targets; the frozen
finger start pose of each hand is in `task.json` (`initial_targets`).

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 28)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 26)`
for `wuji`, at most 6000 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Turn one page of a board book

Turn one page of the board book lying open on the desk in front of the robot. The book shows pages 4 (left) and 5 (right). Turn the next right-hand board, leaf 2 (printed pages 5 and 6), over the spine onto the left stack so that the book shows pages 6 and 7, and take the robot off the book. Every board starts flat on its stack (0.2 mm apart), so the robot has to separate the top board from the board under it itself. Progress is measured by leaf 2's binding hinge angle (joint `leaf_2_binding`: 0 = flat on the right-hand stack, pi = flat on the left-hand stack; it starts at about -0.005 rad, resting on leaf 3). The stages must happen in this order: lifted (angle above 30 degrees), past vertical (above 90 degrees), laid. Laid means, all at the same control: angle above 170 degrees, leaf 2 in physical contact with the left-hand stack (leaf 0, leaf 1 or the left cover), leaf-2 hinge speed at most 0.2 rad/s, every other leaf and both covers within 5 degrees of their start angles, and no contact between the robot (either hand, either arm or the stand) and any part of the book. The laid condition must then hold for 50 consecutive controls (1 s); the episode ends with success at that moment. A partly turned page never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when the book's spine body moves more than 3 cm or rotates more than 10 degrees from its start pose (book shoved or lifted), when any other leaf moves more than 30 degrees from its start angle (a second page turned), when either cover moves more than 30 degrees (the book closing), when the centre of mass of any book part is more than 2 mm below the desk top (z = 0.78 m), or when the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; no object teleports, welds, scripted page motion or direct forces on the book. The book is free on the desk: eight rigid 1.2 mm laminated boards and two covers on passive binding hinges with friction and damping and a small vertical binding compliance. The episode allows at most 3000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

The robot is a fixed Tianji Marvin stand (at the world origin, facing +x; shoulders at (0, +-0.2215, 1.121)) with
two 7-joint arms and a dexterous hand on each wrist; both arms and both hands may be used. Every arm and finger joint
is a position servo in the physics engine under native force bounds (arm servos: stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping
48 N m s/rad, the arms' own torque limits and **no gravity compensation**, so a held target sags slightly under the
arm's weight unless your targets account for it). Lifting, carrying and laying the page down require physical
contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps. The book is not attached to anything: it rests
on the desk under gravity and friction, and a push on its pages moves it unless something holds it.

## Scene
World frame: z up, metres and radians, +x forward from the robot stand, +y to the robot's left. The desk top is the
plane z = 0.78 m (desk x in [0.22, 0.82] m, y in [-0.26, 0.26] m). The board book lies open on the desk as one free
body (`book_spine`, nothing anchors it): its spine runs along the world x axis through y = 0, from x = 0.434 to
x = 0.586 (centre x = 0.51). Every board is a 0.1524 m x 0.1524 m (6 x 6 in), 1.2 mm thick laminated board of 16 g;
the right-hand boards extend from the spine toward -y (the robot's right; fore-edge at y = -0.152), the left-hand
boards toward +y (fore-edge at y = +0.152). Boards hinge at the spine about the world x axis (`<board>_binding`,
passive friction 0.002 N m and damping 0.006 N m s/rad) on a small vertical binding compliance
(`<board>_binding_compliance`, 200 N/m). Hinge-root heights above the desk top: leaf 0 2.0 mm, leaf 1 3.4 mm (left
stack, leaf 1 on top), leaf 2 9.0 mm, leaf 3 7.6 mm, leaf 4 6.2 mm, leaf 5 4.8 mm, leaf 6 3.4 mm, leaf 7 2.0 mm
(right stack, leaf 2 on top), both covers 0.6 mm. **Every board lies flat on its stack, 0.2 mm above the board below
it**: the top board's fore-edge face (1.2 mm tall, at y = -0.152, top at z = 0.7884) sits directly above leaf 3's.
Covers are glued to the spine (hinge spring 0.5 N m/rad). Leaf hinge angles are measured from the flat right-hand
position for right-hand boards (0 = flat right, pi = flat left) and from the flat left-hand position for left-hand
boards (negative = lifted toward the right). At the start the right hand (frame `wrist_stage` / `right_hand_C_MC`,
palm up, index straight) is at about (0.47, -0.44, 0.93) and the left arm hangs parked beside the stand.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`). The robot stands at the world origin facing +x; at the start the left arm is parked and the right hand is palm up beside the book; both arms may be used.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`58` for `sharpa`, `54` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

## Hands

Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`). The robot stands at the world origin facing +x; at the start the left arm is parked and the right hand is palm up beside the book; both arms may be used.
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `58` wide for `sharpa` and `54` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control of all 58 (`sharpa`) or 54 (`wuji`) actuator targets, in radians.
Row layout, `sharpa` (58): 0-6 left arm `SHOULDER_PITCH_L_J1, SHOULDER_ROLL_L_J2, ELBOW_PITCH_L_J3, ELBOW_YAW_L_J4,
WRIST_PITCH_L_J5, WRIST_YAW_L_J6, WRIST_ROLL_L_J7` (actuators `<joint>_target`); 7-13 the same right-arm joints
(`..._R_J1` to `..._R_J7`); 14-35 the left Sharpa Wave fingers `left_thumb_CMC_FE, left_thumb_CMC_AA,
left_thumb_MCP_FE, left_thumb_MCP_AA, left_thumb_IP, left_index_MCP_FE, left_index_MCP_AA, left_index_PIP,
left_index_DIP`, the same four for middle and ring, then `left_pinky_CMC, left_pinky_MCP_FE, left_pinky_MCP_AA,
left_pinky_PIP, left_pinky_DIP`; 36-57 the right Sharpa Wave fingers in the same order (`right_...`).
Row layout, `wuji` (54): 0-13 the same arm targets; 14-33 the left Wuji fingers `l_wuji_l_THJ0..THJ3` (thumb),
`l_wuji_l_FFJ0..FFJ3` (index), `l_wuji_l_MFJ0..MFJ3` (middle), `l_wuji_l_RFJ0..RFJ3` (ring), `l_wuji_l_LFJ0..LFJ3`
(little); 34-53 the right Wuji fingers in the same order (`r_wuji_r_...`). The frozen start row of each hand variant
(arm targets and finger targets) is in `task.json` (`initial_targets`).

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`.

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 58)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 54)`
for `wuji`, at most 3000 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

DexHand: Brush the debris off a boot sole

dexhand-boot-sole-brush-i00 · upstream folder tasks/dexhand/dexhand-boot-sole-brush-i00-standard

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Brush the debris off a boot sole

Brush all six soil clods off the upward-facing sole of the boot into the collection tray. The boot stands sole-up on a fixed boot-rack peg inside the tray (its sole plane is at z = 1.292 m); six small dry soil clods are lodged in its tread, held there by gravity and friction only (no glue or cohesive bond is simulated, so a clod moves as soon as something pushes it). The shoe brush lies bristles-down on the counter: pick it up with the robot's right hand and sweep the sole with the bristles. Success requires, in order: (1) the brush's bristle field touches the boot while the hand touches the brush and the brush does not touch the counter, for at least 10 controls in total; (2) every clod centre lies inside the tray walls (x in [0.366, 0.694] m, y in [-0.184, 0.384] m) below the wall top (z < 0.931 m), however the clod left the sole (swept by the bristles, pushed by the brush's back or knocked off by another clod); (3) then, for 50 consecutive controls (1 s), all six clods stay in the tray with linear speed at most 0.05 m/s while the brush touches neither the boot nor any clod and is withdrawn (bristle-field centre at least 0.04 m above the sole plane, or at least 0.18 m horizontally from the sole centre). The episode ends with success at that moment; fewer than six clods never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when the boot moves more than 0.03 m or tilts more than 0.35 rad from its reset pose; when a clod touches the counter or the floor, falls below the counter top (z < 0.886 m) or leaves the workspace box x in [0.25, 1.2] m, y in [-0.45, 0.45] m, z in [0.886, 1.8] m; when any part of the right hand touches a clod (clods must be brushed, not picked); when the brush touches the floor, the tray or the rack, falls below the counter top, leaves the workspace box, or is released in the air (it touches nothing but clods while its centre of mass sinks faster than 0.2 m/s); when any part of the robot other than its right hand (the stand, the torso, a link of either arm, the parked left hand) touches anything, including the robot itself; or when the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed: no welds, teleports, scripted object motion or applied object forces. The boot, brush and clods are free rigid bodies; the brush's 32 bristle tufts touch the world through one compliant bristle-pad contact proxy (individual fibre bending is not simulated) and the clods are rigid (no fracture or adhesion). The episode allows at most 3000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

You control the right arm and right hand of a fixed Tianji Marvin robot: a stand with two 7-joint arms and a dexterous
hand on each wrist. The stand rests on the floor (z = 0) beside the counter's -y edge, with its base origin at world
(0.147, -0.591, 0.10), facing +y (shoulders 1.121 m above the base origin, at z = 1.221 m; the right shoulder is on
the +x side). The left arm stays parked beside the torso with its hand open; the task is done by the right arm and
hand alone, and no other part of the robot may touch anything. Every arm and finger joint is a position servo inside
the physics engine under native force bounds; arm servos have stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad and **no
gravity compensation** (a held target sags under the arm's weight unless your targets account for it). Grasping,
carrying, brushing and releasing require physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms
physics substeps. The frozen reset lets the boot, the clods, the brush and the arms settle for 0.5 s before control 1.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`); the left arm is parked and only the right arm/hand perform the task.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`58` for `sharpa`, `54` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

Only robot actuator targets are allowed: no welds, teleports, scripted object motion or applied object forces. The boot, brush and clods are free rigid bodies; the brush's 32 bristle tufts touch the world through one compliant bristle-pad contact proxy (individual fibre bending is not simulated) and the clods are rigid (no fracture or adhesion). The episode allows at most 3000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

You control the right arm and right hand of a fixed Tianji Marvin robot: a stand with two 7-joint arms and a dexterous
hand on each wrist. The stand rests on the floor (z = 0) beside the counter's -y edge, with its base origin at world
(0.147, -0.591, 0.10), facing +y (shoulders 1.121 m above the base origin, at z = 1.221 m; the right shoulder is on
the +x side). The left arm stays parked beside the torso with its hand open; the task is done by the right arm and

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`); the left arm is parked and only the right arm/hand perform the task.
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `58` wide for `sharpa` and `54` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control and holds a position target for every actuator, in radians:

- `sharpa` (58 values): 0-6 the left arm `SHOULDER_PITCH_L_J1, SHOULDER_ROLL_L_J2, ELBOW_PITCH_L_J3, ELBOW_YAW_L_J4,
  WRIST_PITCH_L_J5, WRIST_YAW_L_J6, WRIST_ROLL_L_J7` (actuators `<joint>_target`; keep them at the parked start
  values), 7-13 the same right-arm joints (`..._R_J1` to `..._R_J7`), 14-35 the 22 left Sharpa Wave finger targets
  `left_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `left_pinky_DIP`, 36-57 the 22 right Sharpa Wave finger targets `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ...
  `right_pinky_DIP`.
- `wuji` (54 values): 0-13 the same arm targets, 14-33 the 20 left Wuji Hand 2.2 finger targets `l_wuji_l_THJ0..3`,
  `l_wuji_l_FFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_MFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_RFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_LFJ0..3`, 34-53 the 20 right ones
  (`r_wuji_r_...`, same order).

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`. The frozen start targets of each hand are in `task.json`
(`initial_targets`): the right hand starts open, palm down, fingers pointing +y, above the brush (hand frame at about
(0.68, -0.35, 1.115)). The right hand's frame is the body `wrist_stage` on the right flange (fingers along its +z,
palm normal +x, thumb +y), which forward kinematics of the arm joints places in the world.

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 58)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 54)`
for `wuji`, at most 3000 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Stir milk into a mug of coffee with a teaspoon

Mix the milk into the coffee: stir it six times with the teaspoon, then lay the spoon on the worktop beside the mug. The 300 g mug (inner radius 50 mm, 100 mm tall, 8 mm floor) stands upright on the stone worktop (top at z = 0.75 m) with its axis at x = 0.48 m, y = 0.015 m; the coffee, milk already poured, fills it to 64 mm above the mug base (z = 0.814 m). The approved source film (a kinematic demonstration without hands) starts with the teaspoon suspended upright above the rim; here the right hand holds the 35 g teaspoon there, upright, bowl down, in a thumb-index pinch near the top of its handle, with the bowl centre about 0.12 m above the mug base just over the rim (the milk is already poured; the film pours it from an offscreen supply). With the Wuji hand selected (no Wuji start grasp exists yet), the spoon instead starts leaning in the mug (bowl on the mug floor, handle on the rim) and the open Wuji hand hangs about 0.25 m above the mug; the stages are the same. Success requires three stages in order. (1) Submerged in hand: the thumb and at least one other finger touch the spoon, and the bowl centre, bowl tip and bowl neck (23 mm either side of the centre along the spoon) are all between 4 mm and 64 mm above the mug base and within 50 mm of the mug axis. (2) Stirred: the bowl centre revolves at least six full turns about the mug's vertical axis (world frame; net signed angle). The angle accumulates only while the stage-1 condition holds and the bowl centre is at least 8 mm from the axis; a step of more than 0.785 rad in one control is ignored, and the count restarts from zero whenever the bowl leaves the coffee before six turns are complete. (3) Laid down: no part of the hand touches the spoon, the spoon touches the worktop and not the mug, its bowl centre and handle end are both at least 0.10 m from the mug axis horizontally, its axis is within 15 degrees of horizontal, and spoon and mug are still (linear speed at most 0.02 m/s, angular speed at most 0.5 rad/s), for 50 consecutive controls (1 s). The episode ends with success at that moment. The coffee is not simulated: it exerts no force, and the mixing is judged only by these bowl revolutions below its surface. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when the mug tilts more than 10 degrees, slides more than 20 mm or is lifted more than 5 mm; when the spoon touches the floor, or touches the worktop before the six turns are complete; when the spoon touches neither the hand, the mug nor the worktop while its centre of mass falls faster than 0.2 m/s (a dropped spoon cannot be caught again); when the mug touches the floor; when a spoon reference point (bowl centre, tip, neck or handle end) is more than 3 mm below the worktop top or the mug base more than 5 mm below it; when the bowl centre or the handle end leaves the workspace box x in [0, 0.96] m, y in [-0.48, 0.48] m, z in [0.70, 1.60] m; when a fingertip enters the coffee (inside the mug radius below the coffee surface); when an arm link, the stand or the parked left hand touches the mug, the spoon or the worktop; or when the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; no object teleports, grasp welds, scripted object motion or direct object forces. The episode allows at most 3000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

You control the right arm and right hand of a Tianji Marvin dual-arm stand (two 7-joint arms, a dexterous hand on each
wrist; the stand sits at the world origin facing +x, its plate on the floor at z = -0.1 m). The left arm starts parked,
hanging beside the torso, and should stay there. Every arm and finger joint is a position servo in the physics engine
under native force bounds (arm servos: stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad, no gravity compensation, so a held
target sags under the arm's weight unless your targets account for it); stirring and laying the spoon down require
physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps.

## Scene
The mug, the coffee and the teaspoon are the approved T11 kitchen scene: a cream glazed mug with a rounded handle
(pointing +x) on a stone worktop (top at z = 0.75 m, front edge at x = 0.25 m), axis at x = 0.48 m, y = 0.015 m. The
source film (kinematic, without hands) starts with the spoon suspended above the rim; here the right hand holds the
teaspoon there, upright, bowl down, in a thumb-index pinch near the top of its handle, the bowl just above the mug (settled start pose: position (0.452, -0.020, 0.874) m,
quaternion WXYZ (-0.399, 0.006, 0.032, 0.916)). The coffee is a visual surface only: it exerts no force, and the stirring is judged only from the
bowl's revolutions below that surface. Mug and spoon are free rigid bodies that move only through contact and gravity.
Cameras: `overview` (front right of the mug, wide), `closeup` (front right, close) and `top` (looking down the mug axis).

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for sharpa, 20 per hand for wuji); the left arm stays parked and only the right arm and hand perform the task.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`58` for `sharpa`, `54` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

teaspoon there, upright, bowl down, in a thumb-index pinch near the top of its handle, the bowl just above the mug (`task.json` `spoon_pos`, position and quaternion WXYZ, is the

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for sharpa, 20 per hand for wuji); the left arm stays parked and only the right arm and hand perform the task.
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `58` wide for `sharpa` and `54` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control, every actuator target in model order (radians):

- columns 0-6: left arm `SHOULDER_PITCH_L_J1, SHOULDER_ROLL_L_J2, ELBOW_PITCH_L_J3, ELBOW_YAW_L_J4, WRIST_PITCH_L_J5,
  WRIST_YAW_L_J6, WRIST_ROLL_L_J7` (actuators `<joint>_target`); columns 7-13: the same right-arm joints (`..._R_J1` to
  `..._R_J7`);
- `sharpa` (58 values): then the 22 left Sharpa Wave finger targets `left_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `left_pinky_DIP`, then the
  22 right ones `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `right_pinky_DIP`;
- `wuji` (54 values): then the 20 left Wuji Hand 2.2 finger targets `l_wuji_l_THJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_FFJ0..3`,
  `l_wuji_l_MFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_RFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_LFJ0..3`, then the 20 right ones (`r_wuji_r_...`).

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`. The frozen start state of each hand (`task.json`
`initial_qpos`) and its start targets (`initial_targets`) are part of the task; `s.hold_action()` returns the current
targets.

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 58)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 54)`
for `wuji`, at most 3000 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.
