Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Serve a pancake from a frying pan with a spatula

Serve the pancake from the frying pan onto the plate using the kitchen turner (spatula). The turner starts resting on the counter in front of the plate, as in the source scene; pick it up with a hand of the two-arm robot first (both hands start open). The pancake lies in the frying pan, the empty ceramic plate stands beside it on the counter. Only the turner may move the pancake: slide its blade under the pancake, lift it out of the pan on the blade, carry it to the plate, set it down in the plate and withdraw the turner. Success requires three stages in this order. (1) On the blade: the pancake touches the turner blade and no other object (no pan, plate, hand, counter or floor contact), its origin is at least 0.015 m above its starting height and it is tilted at most 30 degrees, for 10 consecutive controls. (2) Over the plate: later, while still touching only the turner, the pancake centre is within 0.058 m (horizontally) of the plate centre and above the plate floor. (3) Served: later, the pancake touches only the plate, its centre is within 0.058 m of the plate centre horizontally (the whole pancake inside the plate's 0.128 m rim radius), it is tilted at most 20 degrees from flat, its linear speed is at most 0.02 m/s and angular speed at most 0.3 rad/s, the turner does not touch it and every point of the blade outline is at least 0.08 m from the pancake centre horizontally (withdrawn); this complete condition must hold for 50 consecutive controls (1 s). The episode ends with success at that moment; skipping or reordering a stage never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 1 ms physics substep with no grace period, when the pancake touches the counter top or the floor, falls freely (touching nothing while its centre of mass moves down faster than 0.35 m/s, i.e. after about 6 mm of free fall) or its origin falls below the counter top (z < 0.85 m), when any part of the robot (hands, arm links, stand) touches the pancake, when the turner touches the floor, falls out of the hand (no hand contact while its centre of mass moves down faster than 0.35 m/s) or its origin falls below the counter top, when the pan or the plate moves more than 0.03 m from its starting position or tilts more than 15 degrees, when the pancake, pan, plate or turner leaves the workspace box x in [0.23, 1.13] m, y in [-0.65, 0.45] m, z in [0.80, 1.50] m, or when the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; no object teleports, grasp welds, scripted object motion or direct object forces. The pancake is a rigid coherent disk and the turner blade bends through three passive spring hinges. The episode allows at most 3000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

The robot is a fixed Tianji Marvin stand at the world origin facing +x, with two 7-joint arms and a dexterous hand
on each wrist (robot id `marvin-bimanual-sharpa-wave`); the right arm and hand do the task and the left arm stays
parked beside the torso. Every arm and finger joint is a position servo in the physics engine under native force
bounds; arm servos have stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad and **no gravity compensation** (a held target
sags by about 1 cm at the hand under load unless your targets account for it). The turner is held only by finger and
palm contact, and the pancake moves only through contact with the turner, the pan and the plate. The controller runs
at 50 Hz, with twenty 1 ms physics substeps per control. World frame: metres and radians, +z up, +x
forward from the robot stand, +y to the robot's left.

## Scene and modelling
The scene reproduces a 22 cm non-stick frying pan (0.90 kg, free on the counter), an OXO flexible kitchen turner
(0.15 kg), a ceramic plate (0.48 kg, free) and one cooked pancake (0.06 kg, about 140 mm across and 9.5 mm thick) on
an oak counter whose top is at z = 0.85 m. Declared simplifications: the pancake is a single rigid coherent body (no
bending, tearing, heat or fluid); the turner's thin steel-core blade is three rigid strips joined by passive spring
hinges (+-0.35 rad); concave pan and plate interiors use convex sector contact shapes. Pair friction coefficients are
estimates: pancake-pan 0.45, pancake-blade 0.20, blade-pan 0.20, pancake-plate 0.60, hand-turner grip 1.2, objects on
the counter 0.7. The turner is not in a hand at the start: as in the source scene it rests on the counter in
front of the plate, at about (0.76, -0.30, 0.878) m with its handle toward -y (handle end and blade base on the counter,
the handle 16 to 30 mm above it); pick it up first. It is held only by contact (there is no weld or attachment).
Physics runs at 1 ms steps, twenty per 50 Hz control.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`); the left arm is parked and only the right arm/hand perform the task.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`58` for `sharpa`, `54` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

## Hands

Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `58` wide for `sharpa` and `54` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control with a position target for every actuator, in model order (`s.actuator_names`):

- columns 0-6: left arm `SHOULDER_PITCH_L_J1, SHOULDER_ROLL_L_J2, ELBOW_PITCH_L_J3, ELBOW_YAW_L_J4, WRIST_PITCH_L_J5,
  WRIST_YAW_L_J6, WRIST_ROLL_L_J7` (each name + `_target`); columns 7-13: the right arm `..._R_J1` to `..._R_J7`;
- `sharpa` (58 values): columns 14-35 the left Sharpa Wave fingers `left_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `left_pinky_DIP`, columns
  36-57 the right Sharpa Wave fingers `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `right_pinky_DIP`;
- `wuji` (54 values): columns 14-33 the left Wuji Hand 2.2 fingers (`l_wuji_*`, vendor order), columns 34-53 the
  right Wuji fingers (`r_wuji_*`).

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`. Both hands start open, the right arm holding its hand
above the counter and the left arm parked (`task.json` `initial_qpos` and `initial_targets` per hand, a settled
state); `s.hold_action()` at reset returns the start targets and keeps that pose.

configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Fold a sheet of paper in half with a permanent crease

Fold the sheet of paper on the table in half: lift its free half over its fixed half, press a permanent crease along the marked center line, take the hand away, and leave the folded sheet lying on the table. The 160 x 100 mm sheet (1.28 g) lies flat on the table top. Its left half is glued to a backing patch next to a dark clamp and cannot move; the right half is free, and its last 25 mm overhang the table edge. Success requires 100 consecutive 50 Hz control samples (2 s) in which no part of the hand touches the paper and all of these hold: fold angle of the free half above 2.6 rad, permanent (plastic) crease on the center line above 2.2 rad on average with at least 90% of its hinges above 2.2 rad, free edge within 18 mm of the fixed edge, stretch below 8%, and the whole sheet over the table top: every paper vertex within the table's extent (x from -0.345 to 0.135 m, y from -0.30 to 0.30 m) and at most 2 mm below the table top (z >= 0.298 m). The episode ends with that success, or fails immediately and permanently if any paper vertex sinks more than 10 mm below the table top (z < 0.29 m, for example bent down over the table edge) or leaves the workspace box (x from -0.03 to 0.19 m, y from -0.09 to 0.09 m, z <= 0.45 m), if the paper stretches by more than 8%, or the simulation becomes unstable. A fold that springs back, a crease that is not permanent, or a hand still touching the paper is not a success. Only the robot's motor targets act on the paper; there are no grasp welds, scripted paper motion or applied forces. The episode allows at most 1500 controls at 50 Hz (30 s).

A dexterous hand on a six-DoF wrist positioning stage is your robot. The wrist stage is position actuated in the
physics engine; folding and creasing need physical contact. Physics runs at 0.5 ms (40 substeps per 20 ms control),
and the controller runs at 50 Hz.

## Scene (world frame, metres, z up)
- Table top at z = 0.30 m, spanning x from -0.345 to 0.135 m (the edge on the hand's side) and y from -0.30 to
  0.30 m. Fail-fast limits on every paper vertex, checked every 0.5 ms: z >= 0.29 m (10 mm below the table top)
  and inside the workspace box x -0.03..0.19 m, y -0.09..0.09 m, z <= 0.45 m. At success every vertex must lie
  within the table's x/y extent and at z >= 0.298 m (2 mm tolerance below the table top).
- The sheet starts flat at z = 0.3012 m, spanning x from 0 to 0.16 m and y from -0.05 to 0.05 m. The half with
  x <= 0.08 m is glued down and never moves; the fold line is at x = 0.08 m (an orange guide line marks it). A fold
  brings the free edge (x = 0.16 m) back over the glued edge (x = 0): the free half rotates by more than 2.6 rad about
  the fold line, upward and over.
- The paper is a passive elastic/plastic sheet: it bends elastically about 0.5 rad beyond its rest shape and then
  yields, so a crease becomes permanent only when the paper is bent well past its current rest shape, and a fold
  that is merely held springs partly back when released. Contact compliance gives it an effective thickness of 0.7 mm.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
The first six targets of a row drive the wrist stage that carries the hand: `wrist_x`, `wrist_y`, `wrist_z` (metres, world frame) and `wrist_rx`, `wrist_ry`, `wrist_rz` (radians, serial XYZ joints); the finger targets follow in the hand's native actuator order. Sharpa starts in a near-edge pregrasp; Wuji starts at the same six wrist targets with its fingers curled clear of the paper.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`28` for `sharpa`, `26` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

- Table top at z = 0.30 m, spanning x from -0.345 to 0.135 m (the edge on the hand's side) and y from -0.30 to

replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. The
replay stops at the first success or failure, so rows after it are not executed. Object poses, configuration
overrides, pickled arrays and success claims in the archive are not read. Save a deliverable early and keep
improving it; the file present when the time budget ends is graded.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Align and staple three paper sheets

Square up three loose A5 sheets and staple them at a corner with the desk stapler, using the dexterous hand on the right arm of a fixed two-arm robot (the left arm stays parked). The sheets lie as a misaligned stack (each upper sheet shifted toward +x) with the bottom sheet's corner resting on the stapler's anvil mouth and the far edge on the desk. Slide the stack into the stapler throat against the stapler's paper stop, square the sheets, press the stapler head through its full stroke onto the stack and let it spring back. Stages, in order: (1) aligned: every corner of sheets 1 and 2 within 2.0 mm of the matching corner of sheet 0 (in sheet 0's plane), the sheets stacked in order (each 0.25-1.5 mm above the one below, along sheet 0's normal) and sheets 0-1 and 1-2 in contact; (2) in the throat: with (1), the staple point (stapler base frame (0.063, 0, 0.012) m, on the anvil under the driver blade) lies inside every sheet 3-30 mm from both edges of one corner and every sheet mid-plane is 0-6 mm above it; (3) pressed: with (1) and (2), the head hinge within 0.01 rad of its bottom stop (0.1701 rad) and the driver blade touching the top sheet; (4) released: after (3), with (1) and (2), the head back up (hinge <= 0.02 rad), no robot contact (either hand or any arm link) with any sheet or the stapler and every sheet's centre of mass slower than 0.02 m/s for 50 consecutive controls (1 s). The episode ends with success at that moment; partial completion never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when a sheet centre falls below z = 0.77925 m (1 mm under its resting height on the desk top) or any sheet corner below z = 0.765 m, a sheet centre leaves the desk (x 0.25-0.99 m, y -0.36-0.36 m) or the workspace box (x 0.2-1.1 m, y -0.45-0.45 m, z 0.70-1.20 m), a sheet or the stapler touches the floor or a desk leg, a sheet or the stapler has no contact at all while its centre of mass falls faster than 0.2 m/s, the stapler base moves more than 3 cm horizontally from its reset position or tilts more than 0.26 rad, an arm link or the robot stand (anything of the robot but the two hands) touches the desk, the stapler or a sheet, or the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. Only arm-joint and finger actuator targets are allowed. The head's return spring needs about 10 N pressed 8 cm in front of its hinge to start the stroke and about 25 N at the bottom stop. Sheets are 0.5 mm rigid plates (real A5 size and mass); staple formation is not simulated. At most 6000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

You control a fixed Tianji Marvin robot: a stand with two 7-joint arms and a dexterous hand on each wrist. The right
arm and its hand suffice for the task; the left arm starts parked beside the stand (hanging straight down) and may stay
there (using it is allowed; every robot contact counts as hand contact). Every arm and finger joint is a position servo inside MuJoCo (implicitfast, 2 ms physics step). Arm servos have
stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad and the arms' own torque limits (shoulder 108, elbow 66, wrist 18 N m), and
**no gravity compensation**: a held target sags by about 1 cm at the hand unless your targets account for it. Pushing,
pressing and releasing require physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`); the left arm is parked and only the right arm/hand perform the task.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`58` for `sharpa`, `54` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

## Scene (frozen instance, world frame)
World frame: z up, metres and radians. The floor is at z = 0. The robot's stand origin is at (0.58, -0.66, 0.10) with
its base plate on the floor, beside the desk's -y edge, facing the desk diagonally (heading 135 deg: toward -x and +y);
the right shoulder is at about (0.737, -0.503, 1.221) and the left at (0.423, -0.817, 1.221); the right hand's mount
starts at (0.80, -0.22, 1.02) with the fingers pointing down. The desk top is at z = 0.78 m and spans x 0.25-0.99 m, y -0.36-0.36 m
(friction: paper on paper 0.4, paper on desk 0.15, paper on the chrome anvil and stop 0.1). The NOVUS B2-style desk
stapler is a free body (0.173 kg) whose base origin is at (0.575, -0.100, 0.783) with its nose toward +x (the source
scene's pose). Its anvil top is at z = 0.795 m; the staple point (base frame (0.063, 0, 0.012) m) is at
(0.638, -0.100, 0.795) in the reset pose. A steel paper stop (insertion guide) stands behind the anvil: its front face
is at base-frame x = 0.0525 m (world x = 0.6275 m) for |y - y_base| <= 0.012 m, z 0.790-0.800 m; a stack whose corner
is fed against it puts the staple point about 10.5 mm inside both edges. The handle with its driver blade turns on one
passive hinge about the base-frame y axis at (-0.052, 0, 0.020): return spring 7.0 N m/rad with 0.115 rad preload
against the open stop (0 rad), bottom stop 0.1701 rad (the blade 0.2 mm into a three-sheet stack lying on the anvil).
The handle top is about 6.6 cm above the desk; pressed 8 cm in front of the hinge, the head needs about 10 N to start
moving and about 25 N at the bottom stop. The magazine is rigid with the base.

The three sheets are rigid A5 plates (0.210 x 0.148 m, 0.5 mm thick, 2.5 g each), indexed bottom (0) to top (2). At
reset they rest as a loose, misaligned stack: the bottom sheet's (-x, -y) corner lies on the anvil mouth in front of
the paper stop, its +x edge on the desk; sheets 1 and 2 are shifted 4 mm and 8 mm toward +x. Rest poses (centre; all
three pitched 0.0733 rad about +y, i.e. the -x end raised, yaw 0): sheet 0 (0.7440, -0.0360, 0.7879),
sheet 1 (0.7480, -0.0356, 0.7881), sheet 2 (0.7520, -0.0364, 0.7883).

Simplifications relative to the source scene (T36), stated plainly: the sheets start with the corner already at the
throat mouth instead of lying flat on the desk (rigid thin sheets cannot be picked up from a flat desk by the modelled
fingertips; the hand only slides the stack in); the paper stop is an added part (the real NOVUS B2 has none; it squares
the stack, which the fingertips cannot do on their own against a flat desk); staple legs, piercing and clinching are
not simulated: "stapled" means the head pressed through its full stroke onto the aligned, inserted stack and released;
the sheets are 0.5 mm thick rigid plates (the source's sheets are 0.1 mm), with the real A5 size and mass.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control, in `s.actuator_names` order (radians):

- columns 0-6: left arm `SHOULDER_PITCH_L_J1, SHOULDER_ROLL_L_J2, ELBOW_PITCH_L_J3, ELBOW_YAW_L_J4, WRIST_PITCH_L_J5,
  WRIST_YAW_L_J6, WRIST_ROLL_L_J7` (actuators `<joint>_target`); columns 7-13: the same right-arm joints (`..._R_J1` to
  `..._R_J7`);
- `sharpa` (58 values): columns 14-35 the left Sharpa Wave fingers `left_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `left_pinky_DIP`, columns
  36-57 the right Sharpa Wave fingers `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `right_pinky_DIP`;
- `wuji` (54 values): columns 14-33 the left Wuji Hand 2.2 fingers `l_wuji_l_THJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_FFJ0..3`,
  `l_wuji_l_MFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_RFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_LFJ0..3`, columns 34-53 the right ones (`r_wuji_r_...`).

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`. Both hands start from the same arm pose; the frozen start
row of each hand is in `task.json` (`initial_targets`). No inverse kinematics is supplied: `s.model` / `s.data` give
the arm's kinematics (the right hand's mount body is `wrist_stage`).

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 58)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 54)`
for `wuji`, at most 6000 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

## Scene (frozen instance, world frame)
World frame: z up, metres and radians. The floor is at z = 0. The robot's stand origin is at (0.58, -0.66, 0.10) with
its base plate on the floor, beside the desk's -y edge, facing the desk diagonally (heading 135 deg: toward -x and +y);
the right shoulder is at about (0.737, -0.503, 1.221) and the left at (0.423, -0.817, 1.221); the right hand's mount
starts at (0.80, -0.22, 1.02) with the fingers pointing down. The desk top is at z = 0.78 m and spans x 0.25-0.99 m, y -0.36-0.36 m
(friction: paper on paper 0.4, paper on desk 0.15, paper on the chrome anvil and stop 0.1). The NOVUS B2-style desk
stapler is a free body (0.173 kg) whose base origin is at (0.575, -0.100, 0.783) with its nose toward +x (the source
scene's pose). Its anvil top is at z = 0.795 m; the staple point (base frame (0.063, 0, 0.012) m) is at
(0.638, -0.100, 0.795) in the reset pose. A steel paper stop (insertion guide) stands behind the anvil: its front face
is at base-frame x = 0.0525 m (world x = 0.6275 m) for |y - y_base| <= 0.012 m, z 0.790-0.800 m; a stack whose corner
is fed against it puts the staple point about 10.5 mm inside both edges. The handle with its driver blade turns on one
passive hinge about the base-frame y axis at (-0.052, 0, 0.020): return spring 7.0 N m/rad with 0.115 rad preload
against the open stop (0 rad), bottom stop 0.1701 rad (the blade 0.2 mm into a three-sheet stack lying on the anvil).
The handle top is about 6.6 cm above the desk; pressed 8 cm in front of the hinge, the head needs about 10 N to start
moving and about 25 N at the bottom stop. The magazine is rigid with the base.

The three sheets are rigid A5 plates (0.210 x 0.148 m, 0.5 mm thick, 2.5 g each), indexed bottom (0) to top (2). At
reset they rest as a loose, misaligned stack: the bottom sheet's (-x, -y) corner lies on the anvil mouth in front of
the paper stop, its +x edge on the desk; sheets 1 and 2 are shifted 4 mm and 8 mm toward +x. Rest poses (centre; all
three pitched 0.0733 rad about +y, i.e. the -x end raised, yaw 0): sheet 0 (0.7440, -0.0360, 0.7879),
sheet 1 (0.7480, -0.0356, 0.7881), sheet 2 (0.7520, -0.0364, 0.7883); exact values in `task.json` `sheets[i].pose` (position, wxyz quaternion).

Simplifications relative to the source scene (T36), stated plainly: the sheets start with the corner already at the
throat mouth instead of lying flat on the desk (rigid thin sheets cannot be picked up from a flat desk by the modelled
fingertips; the hand only slides the stack in); the paper stop is an added part (the real NOVUS B2 has none; it squares
the stack, which the fingertips cannot do on their own against a flat desk); staple legs, piercing and clinching are
not simulated: "stapled" means the head pressed through its full stroke onto the aligned, inserted stack and released;
the sheets are 0.5 mm thick rigid plates (the source's sheets are 0.1 mm), with the real A5 size and mass.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Hang a large picture on two wall hooks

Hang the framed picture on the two wall hooks. The free 2.0 kg frame (52 x 52 x 6 cm) stands upright on a console; two brass picture hooks are installed on the wall and two D-rings on passive hinges are screwed to the back of the frame. Lift the frame off the console with both hands, engage BOTH D-rings on their matching hooks (left ring on the left hook, right ring on the right hook), then let go: the picture must hang still and level from both hooks with no hand touching it. Success requires, in this order: (1) lift-off: the frame origin (the centre of its bottom edge) at least 0.02 m above its start height z = 0.72 m and no contact with the console; (2) engagement: both rings threaded on their own hooks (the hook's load saddle passes through the ring's D loop, with the ring between the hook's upturned lip and the wall; a ring resting on top of the lip does not count) and each ring touching its hook; (3) a released hang for 50 consecutive controls (1 s): both rings threaded, each hook carrying at least 20 % of the frame's weight vertically through its ring and both hooks together at least 85 %, no hand touching the frame, no frame contact with the console or the floor, the frame's top edge level within 3 degrees, its tilt from upright at most 0.10 rad, its centre-of-mass speed at most 0.02 m/s and its angular speed at most 0.15 rad/s. The episode ends with success at that moment; one engaged hook, or rings left on the hook lips, never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when the frame touches the floor, when its origin leaves the workspace box x in [0.20, 0.76] m, y in [-0.45, 0.45] m, z in [0.60, 1.30] m, when it tilts more than 0.6 rad from upright, when after lift-off its origin falls more than 0.01 m below its start height, when after both rings were engaged no hand touches the frame while a ring is not threaded (it fell off a hook), when an arm, torso or stand link of the robot touches anything (only the hands may make contact), or when the physics becomes unstable; and when after lift-off the frame is held by nothing (no hand contact, no console contact and not hanging threaded on both hooks with both rings touching them): at the end of any control, or at any substep where its centre of mass is also moving down faster than 0.2 m/s (dropped, even if caught again, released early, dangling from one hook or resting on the hook lips). Later actions cannot undo a failure. Only the robot's actuator targets (14 arm joints and the fingers of both hands) are allowed; no grasp welds, scripted object motion or forces on the frame. The episode allows at most 3000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

You control a fixed dual-arm robot (Tianji Marvin: two 7-joint arms on a stand) with a dexterous hand on each wrist. The arm joints and the fingers are position actuated in the physics engine under native force bounds;
the frame moves only through contact, gravity and its two passive ring hinges, so lifting, carrying,
hooking and releasing all require physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps.

## Scene (world frame: metres, z up, x pointing into the wall)
- Wall face at x = 0.74. Two installed brass picture hooks at (0.74, +0.255, 1.38) (left) and (0.74, -0.255, 1.38)
  (right): a back strap on the wall, a 6 mm wide load saddle (top face at z = 1.3805) projecting 12 mm from the wall,
  and an upturned 10 mm lip (1 mm wire radius, axis at x = 0.728) at its end.
- Console top at z = 0.72, spanning x 0.35 to 0.65 and y -0.19 to 0.19; the console stands on its two rear legs
  (x = 0.615) so that the robot stand's base plate fits under its front half.
- The frame: 0.52 m wide (y), 0.52 m tall (z), 0.06 m deep (x), 2.0 kg plus two 6 g D-rings; its origin is the centre
  of its bottom edge and it starts upright at (0.50, 0, 0.72), print facing the room (-x). Each D-ring hinges about the
  frame's y axis at frame-local (0.033, +-0.255, 0.478) (3 mm behind the back face, on the side rails) and can swing
  from upright (0 rad) up to 1 rad toward the wall; its D loop (2 mm brass wire) is 18 mm wide and 20 mm tall. Felt
  bumpers sit on the back of the bottom corners.
- The robot stand faces the wall (+x) in front of the console, its base origin at (0.18, 0.00, 0.20): it stands on a
  0.10 m plinth exactly under its base plate; the shoulders are 1.121 m above the base origin, at y = +-0.2215. Only
  the hands may touch anything: any contact of an arm, torso or stand link with the frame, the hooks, the wall, the
  console, the floor or the other hand ends the episode (`robot_collision`).
- At the start both hands hang palm-inward above the frame's side rails, fingers pointing down, thumbs toward the wall. With
  `sharpa` the right hand is the genuine Sharpa Wave right hand and the left hand is a declared mirror image of it (the
  right model reflected, same joints, ranges and force limits); with `wuji` both are the manufacturer's left and right
  Wuji Hand 2.2 models.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7, radians), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`: the genuine right Sharpa Wave on the right flange and its declared mirror image on the left flange; 20 per hand for `wuji`: the manufacturer's left and right Wuji Hand 2.2). Both arms and both hands perform the task.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`58` for `sharpa`, `54` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).
Full task description (original text, privileged setting; differs from the standard one)
# DexHand: Hang a large picture on two wall hooks

Hang the framed picture on the two wall hooks. The free 2.0 kg frame (52 x 52 x 6 cm) stands upright on a console; two brass picture hooks are installed on the wall and two D-rings on passive hinges are screwed to the back of the frame. Lift the frame off the console with both hands, engage BOTH D-rings on their matching hooks (left ring on the left hook, right ring on the right hook), then let go: the picture must hang still and level from both hooks with no hand touching it. Success requires, in this order: (1) lift-off: the frame origin (the centre of its bottom edge) at least 0.02 m above its start height z = 0.72 m and no contact with the console; (2) engagement: both rings threaded on their own hooks (the hook's load saddle passes through the ring's D loop, with the ring between the hook's upturned lip and the wall; a ring resting on top of the lip does not count) and each ring touching its hook; (3) a released hang for 50 consecutive controls (1 s): both rings threaded, each hook carrying at least 20 % of the frame's weight vertically through its ring and both hooks together at least 85 %, no hand touching the frame, no frame contact with the console or the floor, the frame's top edge level within 3 degrees, its tilt from upright at most 0.10 rad, its centre-of-mass speed at most 0.02 m/s and its angular speed at most 0.15 rad/s. The episode ends with success at that moment; one engaged hook, or rings left on the hook lips, never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when the frame touches the floor, when its origin leaves the workspace box x in [0.20, 0.76] m, y in [-0.45, 0.45] m, z in [0.60, 1.30] m, when it tilts more than 0.6 rad from upright, when after lift-off its origin falls more than 0.01 m below its start height, when after both rings were engaged no hand touches the frame while a ring is not threaded (it fell off a hook), when an arm, torso or stand link of the robot touches anything (only the hands may make contact), or when the physics becomes unstable; and when after lift-off the frame is held by nothing (no hand contact, no console contact and not hanging threaded on both hooks with both rings touching them): at the end of any control, or at any substep where its centre of mass is also moving down faster than 0.2 m/s (dropped, even if caught again, released early, dangling from one hook or resting on the hook lips). Later actions cannot undo a failure. Only the robot's actuator targets (14 arm joints and the fingers of both hands) are allowed; no grasp welds, scripted object motion or forces on the frame. The episode allows at most 3000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

You control a fixed dual-arm robot (Tianji Marvin: two 7-joint arms on a stand) with a dexterous hand on each wrist. The arm joints and the fingers are position actuated in the physics engine under native force bounds;
the frame moves only through contact, gravity and its two passive ring hinges, so lifting, carrying,
hooking and releasing all require physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps.

## Scene (world frame: metres, z up, x pointing into the wall)
- Wall face at x = 0.74. Two installed brass picture hooks at (0.74, +0.255, 1.38) (left) and (0.74, -0.255, 1.38)
  (right): a back strap on the wall, a 6 mm wide load saddle (top face at z = 1.3805) projecting 12 mm from the wall,
  and an upturned 10 mm lip (1 mm wire radius, axis at x = 0.728) at its end.
- Console top at z = 0.72, spanning x 0.35 to 0.65 and y -0.19 to 0.19; the console stands on its two rear legs
  (x = 0.615) so that the robot stand's base plate fits under its front half.
- The frame: 0.52 m wide (y), 0.52 m tall (z), 0.06 m deep (x), 2.0 kg plus two 6 g D-rings; its origin is the centre
  of its bottom edge and it starts upright at (0.50, 0, 0.72), print facing the room (-x). Each D-ring hinges about the
  frame's y axis at frame-local (0.033, +-0.255, 0.478) (3 mm behind the back face, on the side rails) and can swing
  from upright (0 rad) up to 1 rad toward the wall; its D loop (2 mm brass wire) is 18 mm wide and 20 mm tall. Felt
  bumpers sit on the back of the bottom corners.
- The robot stand faces the wall (+x) in front of the console, its base origin at (0.18, 0.00, 0.20): it stands on a
  0.10 m plinth exactly under its base plate; the shoulders are 1.121 m above the base origin, at y = +-0.2215. Only
  the hands may touch anything: any contact of an arm, torso or stand link with the frame, the hooks, the wall, the
  console, the floor or the other hand ends the episode (`robot_collision`).
- At the start both hands hang palm-inward above the frame's side rails, fingers pointing down, thumbs toward the wall.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7, radians), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`: the genuine right Sharpa Wave on the right flange and its declared mirror image on the left flange; 20 per hand for `wuji`: the manufacturer's left and right Wuji Hand 2.2). Both arms and both hands perform the task.
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `58` wide for `sharpa` and `54` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control: the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (radians) `SHOULDER_PITCH_L_J1_target,
SHOULDER_ROLL_L_J2_target, ELBOW_PITCH_L_J3_target, ELBOW_YAW_L_J4_target, WRIST_PITCH_L_J5_target,
WRIST_YAW_L_J6_target, WRIST_ROLL_L_J7_target`, then the same seven for the right arm (`..._R_J1_target` ...
`..._R_J7_target`), then the left hand's finger targets and the right hand's, in radians:

- `sharpa`: 58 values, 22 Sharpa Wave finger targets per hand: `left_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `left_pinky_DIP`, then
  `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `right_pinky_DIP`. The right hand is the genuine Sharpa Wave right hand; the left hand is a
  declared mirror image of it (the right model reflected across its palm's sagittal plane, same joints, ranges and
  force limits), not a separate manufacturer left-hand model.
- `wuji`: 54 values, 20 Wuji Hand 2.2 finger targets per hand: `l_wuji_l_THJ0..3, l_wuji_l_FFJ0..3, l_wuji_l_MFJ0..3,
  l_wuji_l_RFJ0..3, l_wuji_l_LFJ0..3`, then the same for `r_wuji_r_` (the manufacturer's left and right models).

Arm servos: kp 700 N m/rad, kv 48 N m s/rad, force limits 108 / 108 / 66 / 66 / 18 / 18 / 18 N m (J1 ... J7), no
gravity compensation (a loaded arm sags unless you correct it). Each hand sits rigidly on its arm's flange (bodies
`l_wrist_stage` / `r_wrist_stage`; fingers along the flange +z, palm normal +x, thumb +y for the right hand). No IK
primitive is supplied. Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`; the frozen start targets (arm pose
with the hands above the frame, open fingers) are in `task.json` `initial_targets`.

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 58)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 54)`
for `wuji`, at most 3000 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Place a two-handle pot into a shelf

A fixed dual-arm robot (two 7-joint arms, a dexterous hand on each wrist) stands at a kitchen worktop. A freely moving 1 kg two-handle stockpot (286 mm vessel diameter, 438 mm across its two loop handles) rests on the worktop; an open kitchen shelf is to the robot's left. Grasp the pot by its two handles, lift it with both hands, carry it into the shelf compartment and set it down upright on the shelf board at the target, then open both hands and withdraw them. The pot must never be dropped, tipped over, knocked against the furniture, the floor or a non-hand robot link, or leave its support while no hand carries it. Only the robot's position-controlled joint targets act on the world: there are no attachments, object actuators, scripted object motion or applied forces.

The service executes and records every row you submit, and the first failure ends the episode, so check each chunk
before you send it: a reset starts a new episode from the same start, 20 times at most, and only the last episode is
graded (see `## Episodes and resets`). The service grades the episode it ran; there is no trajectory to hand in. Keep
working until an episode has succeeded.

## Robot, scene and control
The robot is a fixed Tianji Marvin stand with two 7-joint arms and a dexterous hand on each wrist. Every arm and finger
joint is a position servo inside MuJoCo 3.4.0 (CPU, implicitfast integrator, 2 ms physics step). Arm servos have
stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad, the arms' own torque limits and **no gravity compensation**: a held target
sags under the arm's and the pot's weight unless your targets account for it. Every joint's range and effort limit is in
`spec()["robot_spec"]`. The pot moves only through contact and gravity.

**Control rate: one action row is one 2 ms physics step (500 Hz).** A row holds a position target for every actuator
(radians), applied for exactly one physics step. The service clips targets to the published joint limits and
reports clipping.

World frame: metres, radians, seconds; +z up, +x forward from the robot stand, +y to the robot's left; quaternions are
wxyz. Scene facts: the worktop top is at z = 0.75; the pot is upright on it with its base centre at
(0.52, -0.05, 0.75) and its two loop handles along the world y axis (handle loops 0.13 to 0.22 m from the pot axis,
0.133 to 0.187 m above the base); the open shelf's board top is at z = 0.79 and spans x from -0.14 to 1.14 and y from
0.12 to 0.84; the compartment is closed by side walls (inner faces x = -0.14 and x = 1.14), a back wall
(inner face y = 0.84) and a top board (underside z = 1.465), and opens toward -y. The target for the pot's base
centre is (0.46, 0.31, 0.79).

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`); one row is one 2 ms physics step.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`58` for `sharpa`, `54` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

Row layout, `sharpa` (58): 0-6 left arm `SHOULDER_PITCH_L_J1, SHOULDER_ROLL_L_J2, ELBOW_PITCH_L_J3, ELBOW_YAW_L_J4,
WRIST_PITCH_L_J5, WRIST_YAW_L_J6, WRIST_ROLL_L_J7` (actuators `<joint>_target`); 7-13 the same right-arm joints
(`..._R_J1` to `..._R_J7`); 14-35 the left Sharpa Wave fingers `l_hand_thumb_CMC_FE, l_hand_thumb_CMC_AA,
l_hand_thumb_MCP_FE, l_hand_thumb_MCP_AA, l_hand_thumb_IP, l_hand_index_MCP_FE, l_hand_index_MCP_AA, l_hand_index_PIP,
l_hand_index_DIP`, the same four for middle and ring, then `l_hand_pinky_CMC, l_hand_pinky_MCP_FE, l_hand_pinky_MCP_AA,
l_hand_pinky_PIP, l_hand_pinky_DIP`; 36-57 the right Sharpa Wave fingers in the same order (`r_hand_...`).
Row layout, `wuji` (54): 0-13 the same arm targets; 14-33 the left Wuji fingers `l_wuji_l_THJ0..THJ3` (thumb),
`l_wuji_l_FFJ0..FFJ3` (index), `l_wuji_l_MFJ0..MFJ3` (middle), `l_wuji_l_RFJ0..RFJ3` (ring), `l_wuji_l_LFJ0..LFJ3`
(little); 34-53 the right Wuji fingers in the same order (`r_wuji_r_...`). Both hands start open at the same arm pose.

## Success
The service evaluates the predicate after every physics step it executes, and that is the graded verdict.
Success needs both stages, in order:
1. **Bimanual carry**: for at least 0.5 s in total (250 steps) the pot's base is above z = 0.785 m, neither the worktop
   nor the shelf bears on it, and each hand pushes it upward with at least 0.5 N (sum of the vertical components of
   that hand's contact forces on the pot).
2. **Released on the shelf**, held for 2.0 s (1,000 consecutive steps) after stage 1, every condition at every step:
   - the pot's base centre is within 0.04 m horizontally of (0.46, 0.31) and within 0.012 m of z = 0.79;
   - upright: the angle between the pot's axis and +z is at most 0.10 rad;
   - at rest: linear speed at most 0.03 m/s and angular speed at most 0.15 rad/s;
   - resting on the shelf alone: the shelf board bears on the pot and nothing else touches it;
   - fully inside the compartment: the vessel's circular footprint (radius 0.143 m around the base centre) lies on
     the shelf board, and every part of the pot, handles included, is between the side walls, in front of the back
     wall, below the top board and at most 0.05 m in front of the board's front edge (y >= 0.07). This 50 mm
     open-front allowance exists because the 438 mm handle span lies along y: at the target the front handle
     reaches about 34 mm past the board's front edge (y = 0.12); the side walls, back wall and top board are strict;
   - both hands released and withdrawn: every hand collision surface is at least 0.04 m from the pot.

The episode ends as a success when the hold completes; the service then refuses further actions. Anything less
(pot still held, placed but not released, released outside the target, hold not completed when the episode ends) is a
failure.

## Immediate failure
These are the only early failures. The first one that occurs ends the episode as a failure; later rows cannot recover
it. "Touches" means a contact with a normal force of at least 0.02 N unless stated otherwise.
1. Fell: the pot's base (its bottom centre) is below z = 0.70 m (worktop top 0.75 m, shelf board top 0.79 m).
2. Left the workspace: the pot's base leaves the box x in [-0.10, 1.10] m, y in [-0.50, 0.85] m, z <= 1.45 m.
3. Tipped: the pot's axis is more than 0.5 rad from +z.
4. Dropped: the pot's base moves downward faster than 0.6 m/s (about a 2 cm free fall), or the pot touches nothing
   at all (no hand, worktop or shelf-board contact of any force) for more than 0.06 s (30 consecutive steps).
5. Knocked into something: the pot touches anything other than the two hands, the worktop and the shelf board (the
   floor, the cabinet side walls, back wall, top board or bases, a non-hand robot link).
6. Robot collision: a robot link touches the furniture or the floor, or two robot parts collide (contacts within one
   hand excepted).
7. Hand penetration: a hand penetrates the pot by more than 3 mm.
8. Joint limit: a robot joint exceeds its range by more than 0.005 rad.
9. Unstable physics (MuJoCo reports a bad position, velocity or acceleration).
10. Budget: 30000 physics steps (60 s of simulated time) pass without success.

Everything else is allowed and only matters through the success conditions. In particular the pot may be set back
down on the worktop (or rest on it with one side while a hand still holds the other), touch the worktop or the shelf
board again, and be regrasped any number of times, provided none of the conditions above occurs; the 0.5 s of
bimanual carry is counted over the whole episode, and the 2 s released hold must be consecutive.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

# DexHand: Place a two-handle pot into a shelf

A fixed dual-arm robot (two 7-joint arms, a dexterous hand on each wrist) stands at a kitchen worktop. A freely moving 1 kg two-handle stockpot (286 mm vessel diameter, 438 mm across its two loop handles) rests on the worktop; an open kitchen shelf is to the robot's left. Grasp the pot by its two handles, lift it with both hands, carry it into the shelf compartment and set it down upright on the shelf board at the target, then open both hands and withdraw them. The pot must never be dropped, tipped over, knocked against the furniture, the floor or a non-hand robot link, or leave its support while no hand carries it. Only the robot's position-controlled joint targets act on the world: there are no attachments, object actuators, scripted object motion or applied forces.

Save a valid trajectory early and keep
improving it; do not stop early.

## Robot, scene and control
The robot is a fixed Tianji Marvin stand with two 7-joint arms and a dexterous hand on each wrist. Every arm and finger
joint is a position servo inside MuJoCo 3.4.0 (CPU, implicitfast integrator, 2 ms physics step). Arm servos have
stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad, the arms' own torque limits and **no gravity compensation**: a held target
sags under the arm's and the pot's weight unless your targets account for it. Finger servos and every joint range and
force limit are in `s.model`. The pot moves only through contact and gravity.

**Control rate: one action row is one 2 ms physics step (500 Hz).** A row holds a position target for every actuator
(radians), applied for exactly one physics step. Rows outside `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange` are rejected.

World frame: metres, radians, seconds; +z up, +x forward from the robot stand, +y to the robot's left; quaternions are
wxyz. Scene facts (all also readable from the model): the worktop top is at z = 0.75; the pot is upright on it with its
base centre at (0.52, -0.05, 0.75) and its two loop handles along the world y axis (handle loops 0.13 to 0.22 m from the
pot axis, 0.133 to 0.187 m above the base); the open shelf's board top is at z = 0.79 and spans x from -0.14 to 1.14
and y from 0.12 to 0.84; the compartment is closed by side walls (inner faces x = -0.14 and x = 1.14), a back wall
(inner face y = 0.84) and a top board (underside z = 1.465), and opens toward -y. The target for the pot's base
centre is (0.46, 0.31, 0.79).

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`); one row is one 2 ms physics step.
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `58` wide for `sharpa` and `54` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). l_hand_thumb_MCP_FE, l_hand_thumb_MCP_AA, l_hand_thumb_IP, l_hand_index_MCP_FE, l_hand_index_MCP_AA, l_hand_index_PIP,

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 58)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 54)`
for `wuji`, 1 <= T <= 30000, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these rows in one fresh process, which must succeed. Object poses, success flags, configuration overrides and pickled arrays are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexHand: Install a desktop DDR4 RAM module

Install the DDR4 memory module into the outer DIMM socket of the motherboard (socket_3, the slot nearest the board edge). The module stands upright in a slotted anti-static foam holder on the bench, key notch towards +y; the motherboard is fixed in its service tray and the socket's single moving latch starts open. Pick the module up, keep its keyed orientation, insert it straight into the socket and press it home so that the passive latch snaps closed, then let go. The episode succeeds when these stages have happened in order: (1) picked: the module is out of the holder (no holder contact, its lower edge at least 10 mm above the slit top, z >= 0.851 m) and held by the thumb and at least one other finger; (2) seated: both lower module ends 1.5 to 2.6 mm above the socket base (the 2 mm seating datum), lateral offset of both ends at most 0.5 mm, along-slot offset at most 1.0 mm, the module's height axis within 3 degrees of vertical and its length axis within 3 degrees of the socket's keyed direction (a reversed module never counts); (3) latched: while seated, the moving latch hinge is at most 0.08 rad (closed); and then, for 50 consecutive controls (1 s), the module stays seated and latched with no hand contact on the module or the latch, module speed at most 0.01 m/s and angular speed at most 0.2 rad/s. The episode ends with success at that moment; a partial installation never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when the module touches anything other than the hand, its foam holder or the target socket (the bench, the service tray, the motherboard and its components, the other three sockets, the floor), when the module is unsupported (touches nothing) while its centre of mass falls faster than 0.2 m/s, or has fallen freely more than 5 cm (no drop-and-catch), when any lower module corner drops below the bench top (z < 0.825 m) or a lower module end inside the socket comes closer than 1.2 mm to the socket base (pushed into the 2 mm floor), when the module origin leaves the workspace box x in [0.30, 0.95] m, y in [-0.36, 0.34] m, z in [0.826, 1.25] m, or when the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; no object teleports, grasp welds, scripted object motion or direct module forces. The episode allows at most 3000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure. The socket throat is the source's 1.66 mm (module 1.27 mm).

You control one dexterous hand mounted on a six-DoF wrist positioning stage (three prismatic and three serial revolute
joints, no arm). The stage and the fingers are position actuated in the physics engine under native force bounds;
grasping, carrying, inserting and releasing require physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics
substeps.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Both hands hang from the same six-axis wrist stage, with the same wrist joints, ranges, gains and start targets; the wrist targets are the world position (m) and serial XYZ angles (rad) of the hand mount.
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`28` for `sharpa`, `26` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

# DexHand: Install a desktop DDR4 RAM module

Install the DDR4 memory module into the outer DIMM socket of the motherboard (socket_3, the slot nearest the board edge). The module stands upright in a slotted anti-static foam holder on the bench, key notch towards +y; the motherboard is fixed in its service tray and the socket's single moving latch starts open. Pick the module up, keep its keyed orientation, insert it straight into the socket and press it home so that the passive latch snaps closed, then let go. The episode succeeds when these stages have happened in order: (1) picked: the module is out of the holder (no holder contact, its lower edge at least 10 mm above the slit top, z >= 0.851 m) and held by the thumb and at least one other finger; (2) seated: both lower module ends 1.5 to 2.6 mm above the socket base (the 2 mm seating datum), lateral offset of both ends at most 0.5 mm, along-slot offset at most 1.0 mm, the module's height axis within 3 degrees of vertical and its length axis within 3 degrees of the socket's keyed direction (a reversed module never counts); (3) latched: while seated, the moving latch hinge is at most 0.08 rad (closed); and then, for 50 consecutive controls (1 s), the module stays seated and latched with no hand contact on the module or the latch, module speed at most 0.01 m/s and angular speed at most 0.2 rad/s. The episode ends with success at that moment; a partial installation never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when the module touches anything other than the hand, its foam holder or the target socket (the bench, the service tray, the motherboard and its components, the other three sockets, the floor), when the module is unsupported (touches nothing) while its centre of mass falls faster than 0.2 m/s, or has fallen freely more than 5 cm (no drop-and-catch), when any lower module corner drops below the bench top (z < 0.825 m) or a lower module end inside the socket comes closer than 1.2 mm to the socket base (pushed into the 2 mm floor), when the module origin leaves the workspace box x in [0.30, 0.95] m, y in [-0.36, 0.34] m, z in [0.826, 1.25] m, or when the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets are allowed; no object teleports, grasp welds, scripted object motion or direct module forces. The episode allows at most 3000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure. The socket throat is the source's 1.66 mm (module 1.27 mm).

You control one dexterous hand mounted on a six-DoF wrist positioning stage (three prismatic and three serial revolute
joints, no arm). The stage and the fingers are position actuated in the physics engine under native force bounds;
grasping, carrying, inserting and releasing require physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms
physics substeps.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Both hands hang from the same six-axis wrist stage, with the same wrist joints, ranges, gains and start targets; the wrist targets are the world position (m) and serial XYZ angles (rad) of the hand mount.
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `28` wide for `sharpa` and `26` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control. The first six entries are the wrist-stage targets, identical for both hands:
`wrist_x, wrist_y, wrist_z` (metres, world position of the hand mount) and `wrist_rx, wrist_ry, wrist_rz` (radians,
serial XYZ joints, not a quaternion). The finger targets follow in native actuator order, in radians:

- `sharpa`: 28 values, the six wrist targets and 22 Sharpa Wave finger targets `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `right_pinky_DIP`.
- `wuji`: 26 values, the same six wrist targets and 20 Wuji Hand 2.2 finger targets `r_wuji_r_THJ0..3`,
  `r_wuji_r_FFJ0..3`, `r_wuji_r_MFJ0..3`, `r_wuji_r_RFJ0..3`, `r_wuji_r_LFJ0..3`.

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`. Both hands start from the same wrist targets (hand above
the bench, fingers pointing down); the frozen finger start pose of each hand is in `task.json` (`initial_targets`).

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 28)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 26)`
for `wuji`, at most 3000 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.

# DexHand: Replace the battery of a TV remote

Replace the battery of a TV remote that lies on the table. The remote's sliding battery door is shut and latched over a one-cell compartment holding an old gray AA cell; a new green AA cell lies on the table and an empty receiving tray stands beside the remote. In this order: (1) release the door latch by pressing the door's spring-loaded thumb tab down and slide the door open until it is at least 0.060 m open (full travel 0.085 m); (2) move the gray cell out of the compartment into the tray, where it must rest on the tray floor: its centre inside the tray's inner box (|x| <= 0.037 m, |y| <= 0.032 m in the tray frame) and at most 0.014 m above the tray origin (the floor top is 0.003 m above the origin; a resting cell's centre is about 0.010 m above it), touching the tray floor, with no hand contact; (3) seat the green cell in the compartment slot with correct polarity: its centre within 5 mm (along the slot), 3 mm (across) and 2 mm (height) of the slot centre, lying on both cradle ribs, and its + end toward the gold contact (cell axis within 10 degrees of the remote's long axis, + end at the gold contact); (4) slide the door shut and let the latch engage: at most 0.002 m open with the thumb tab released (pressed at most 0.0015 m), so its hook sits in front of the latch stop. Then release everything: with no hand contact on the remote, door, tray or either cell, the gray cell still in the tray, the green cell still seated, the door still shut and latched and every task object at rest (linear speed of its body origin <= 0.02 m/s, angular speed <= 0.5 rad/s; for the cells and the tray the origin is the centre of mass), the condition must hold for 50 consecutive controls (1 s). The episode ends with success at that moment; each stage counts only after the previous ones, and partial completion never counts. The episode ends immediately with failure, checked after every 2 ms physics substep, when any cell, the door, the remote or the tray falls below the table top (z < 0.30 m) or leaves the workspace box x in [-0.37, 0.47] m, y in [-0.34, 0.34] m, z in [0.30, 0.80] m, when any of them touches the floor, when the remote slides more than 0.03 m or tilts more than 15 degrees, when the tray slides more than 0.03 m or tilts more than 15 degrees, when the gray cell touches the table top, when the green cell touches the table top again after it has been lifted (lifted: at a control it is clear of the table and its centre is more than 0.01 m above its start height), when a cell without hand contact moves down faster than 0.886 m/s (the speed of a free drop from 0.04 m), or a cell touching nothing at all (no hand, no surface) moves down faster than 0.5 m/s (there is no grace period; a later catch does not undo it), when the parked left arm or the left hand touches the remote, its door, the tray or a cell (left_arm_contact; moving the left arm is not blocked, but the task is done by the right arm and hand), or when the physics becomes unstable; later actions cannot undo a failure. Only robot actuator targets (arm joints and fingers) are allowed; no object teleports, grasp welds, scripted object motion or direct object forces. The episode allows at most 6000 controls at 50 Hz; reaching that limit without success is a failure.

## Scene
World frame: z up, metres and radians; the table top is at z = 0.30 m (the floor is at z = -0.55 m). The remote lies
flat at (0.0, 0.0, 0.32) with its long axis along world x; it is a free rigid body of 0.35 kg (a weighted handset) on
four rubber feet, at the approved scene's size (shell 160 x 64 mm, battery cavity 94 x 52 mm). Its battery door
slides along the remote's -x direction on a passive slide joint (travel 0 to 0.085 m, end stops at both ends, damping
0.1 N s/m, 0.08 N friction loss) and is latched shut: a spring-loaded thumb tab on the door (18 x 18 mm, 3 mm proud
of the door, a passive slide joint pressing down 0 to 5 mm against a 120 N/m spring) carries a hook that sits just in
front of a fixed latch stop at the remote's rear end while the door is shut. The door opens only while the tab is
pressed far enough (about 2.9 to 4.5 mm) for the hook to pass under the stop; it re-latches when it is slid fully
shut and the tab is released. Under the door is a one-cell compartment: the slot centre is at (-0.020, 0.0,
-0.00244) m in the remote frame, the gray cell lies there on two low cradle ribs with its + end toward the gold
contact at the slot's +x end (the silver - contact is at the -x end; 3 mm end play). The green replacement cell (a
23 g rigid cylinder, radius 7 mm, 49 mm long, like the gray one) lies on the table at (0.115, -0.110, 0.307) with its
+ end pointing 20 degrees clockwise from world +x (seen from above). The receiving tray (free rigid body, inner 74 x
64 mm, 18 mm walls) stands at (0.16, 0.10, 0.303). Modelling scope: the compartment holds one cell as in the source
scene; the source's compressible negative spring is not modelled (the terminals are fixed); there is no electrical
simulation. All objects move only through contact and these passive joints.

You control a fixed Tianji Marvin robot standing at the table (stand origin at (-0.45, 0.15, -0.45), facing +x) with
two 7-joint arms and a dexterous hand on each wrist; the right arm and hand do the task, the left arm hangs parked
beside the torso (keep its targets). Every arm and finger joint is a position servo inside MuJoCo 3.4.0 under native
force bounds; the arm servos have stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad and **no gravity compensation** (a held
target sags under the arm's weight unless your targets account for it). Grasping, carrying and releasing require
physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps per control.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`); the left arm is parked and only the right arm/hand perform the task; one row is one 50 Hz control (ten 2 ms physics substeps).
The robot service runs the hand named by `DEXHAND_HAND` on the sim service (default `sharpa`); the agent cannot switch it during an episode. `spec()["hand"]` names it, and `spec()["action_types"]["joint_position"]` gives the row width (`58` for `sharpa`, `54` for `wuji`) and the exact order. The episode record names the hand; the service grades the episode it ran with that hand.

## Episodes and resets
You have **20 resets** (`spec["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0, there is no reset
and the one episode is the run). A reset puts the robot and every object back in the same frozen starting state and
starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended; it takes no simulated time and
returns the start's images and proprioception:
```python
res = r._post("/reset", {"cameras": ["overview"]}, [], 900)   # POST /reset (the 2.2 client has no reset())
res.meta["episode"], res.meta["resets_left"]
```
Once an episode has ended, `submit` raises `EpisodeOver` until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: an
episode you reset away is never graded, a success ends the run at once (no reset after it), and when your time is up
the episode then running is the one graded. The wall clock is the run's and never restarts; `meta["episode"]` and
`meta["resets_left"]` count the episodes (`meta["control_steps"]` is the current episode's,
`meta["control_steps_total"]` all of them).

You control a fixed Tianji Marvin robot standing at the table (stand origin at (-0.45, 0.15, -0.45), facing +x) with
two 7-joint arms and a dexterous hand on each wrist; the right arm and hand do the task, the left arm hangs parked

force bounds; the arm servos have stiffness 700 N m/rad, damping 48 N m s/rad and **no gravity compensation** (a held
target sags under the arm's weight unless your targets account for it). Grasping, carrying and releasing require
physical contact. The controller runs at 50 Hz, with ten 2 ms physics substeps per control.

## Hands
Two genuine manufacturer hand models are available: `sharpa` (Sharpa Wave, 22 finger actuators; the default) and `wuji` (Wuji Hand 2.2, 20 finger actuators). The task, scene, mount, objects and success predicate are the same for both; only one hand is used per episode.
Each row starts with the 14 Marvin arm joint targets (left arm J1-J7, then right arm J1-J7), followed by the left hand's finger targets and then the right hand's (22 per hand for `sharpa`, 20 per hand for `wuji`); the left arm is parked and only the right arm/hand perform the task; one row is one 50 Hz control (ten 2 ms physics substeps).
Choose the hand with `Session(..., hand="wuji")` or the environment variable `DEXHAND_HAND=wuji` (default `sharpa`). Action rows are `58` wide for `sharpa` and `54` wide for `wuji`; `s.actuator_names` gives the exact order. `s.save_trajectory(actions, path)` records the hand in the archive (`hand` member). The verifier rebuilds the scene with the recorded hand (default `sharpa` when the member is absent) and rejects a trajectory whose width does not match that hand; rows are never padded, truncated or converted between hands.

## Action layout
Each row is one 50 Hz control holding a position target for every actuator (radians), in native actuator order:

- `sharpa` (58 values): 0-6 left arm `SHOULDER_PITCH_L_J1, SHOULDER_ROLL_L_J2, ELBOW_PITCH_L_J3, ELBOW_YAW_L_J4,
  WRIST_PITCH_L_J5, WRIST_YAW_L_J6, WRIST_ROLL_L_J7` (actuators `<joint>_target`); 7-13 the same right-arm joints
  (`..._R_J1` to `..._R_J7`); 14-35 the left Sharpa Wave fingers `left_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `left_pinky_DIP`; 36-57 the
  right Sharpa Wave fingers `right_thumb_CMC_FE` ... `right_pinky_DIP`.
- `wuji` (54 values): 0-13 the same arm targets; 14-33 the left Wuji Hand 2.2 fingers `l_wuji_l_THJ0..3`,
  `l_wuji_l_FFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_MFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_RFJ0..3`, `l_wuji_l_LFJ0..3`; 34-53 the right Wuji fingers in the
  same order (`r_wuji_r_...`).

Every target must lie within `s.model.actuator_ctrlrange`. Both hands start from the same arm pose (right hand above
the table near the robot, left arm parked); the frozen start targets of each hand are in `task.json`
(`initial_targets`).

## Deliverable
Save `/app/output/trajectory.npz` with a finite numeric `actions` array of shape `(T, 58)` for `sharpa` or `(T, 54)`
for `wuji`, at most 6000 rows, plus the `hand` member (`s.save_trajectory` writes both), and
`/app/output/gen.py`, the script that produced it. The separate verifier rebuilds the frozen scene with the recorded
hand and replays only these motor targets in one fresh process, which must succeed. A replay stops at the first success or the first failure; later rows are not executed. Object poses,
configuration overrides, pickled arrays and success claims are not deliverables and are never read.
Save the archive compressed (`numpy.savez_compressed`; `s.save_trajectory` does): an archive file larger than 64 MB is rejected with reward 0.
