The agent only gets a client: camera RGB-D + proprioception and joint-target chunks; 20 resets (only the last episode graded), no object poses; the sim service records every episode and grades the last one live (no grading replay).
  • Original environment (the benchmark's own code, MuJoCo 3.3.7, run here in its pinned Docker image): the reference reaches 13 of 40 goals; its 1,083 action rows end there, the result the task's README documents. The start-state hash d2e6cac6ac14 equals the one recorded in the task, two fresh runs give identical arrays, and the unmodified replay entry point returns the same result (end hash 6771248d6c89).
  • The scene without the robot is exported as one file written with full precision (the benchmark has no scene file; its scene is built by code). Compiled alone it equals the original model element by element in MuJoCo 3.3.7 (184 arrays identical, 213 belong to kinds of element only the robot has) and in MuJoCo 3.8.0 (194 arrays identical). Different by construction: quantities that count the robot (mass below the world body, camera and light offsets from the model's centre of mass, the automatic statistics), and the world body's gravity-compensation value, which the original sets through its API, no scene file can carry, and which applies no force.
  • The port's own stepping loop and goal rule, run on the original model in MuJoCo 3.3.7, reproduce the original bit for bit: state, goals reached and goal marker after every control and the final hash, over the reference and three altered action sequences (5,532 controls, one of which ends by the per-goal time limit); restarting from each of the 1,083 recorded states and stepping one control gives exactly zero difference.
  • Under our MuJoCo 3.8.0 the original code needs one guarded line (a flag name that no longer exists). It then gives the recorded start hash and the same reset state, and the port's loop reproduces it bit for bit over 5,049 controls (the reference and the three altered sequences).
  • Both engines compile the same model: 415 of 425 arrays are identical, masses, inertias, geometry and friction included; the 10 others are 9 mesh polygon tables, which the engines build differently, and 1 table of offsets into the file-path buffer (the assets sit at another path on the host). Option entries and flags, read as effective settings, are equal.
  • Outcome of the same reference in our MuJoCo 3.8.0: 0 of 40 goals with the scene as exported, 9 of 40 with MuJoCo's documented opt-out of its newer free-body integration (flag invdiscrete), against 13 of 40 in the original engine.
  • As exported, the two engines compared control by control over 1,083 controls: after the first control the tool pose differs by 1.4e-04; it first differs by more than 1e-9 at control 1, by more than 1e-6 at control 1 and by more than 1e-3 at control 3. Robot joints first differ by more than 1e-12 at control 36 and by more than 1e-3 at control 42; the robot first touches the scene during control 36 in both engines, and before that its joints differ by at most 2.2e-16.
  • With the opt-out, the two engines compared control by control over 1,083 controls: after the first control the tool pose differs by 0; it first differs by more than 1e-9 at control 37, by more than 1e-6 at control 37 and by more than 1e-3 at control 41. Robot joints first differ by more than 1e-12 at control 37 and by more than 1e-3 at control 40; the robot first touches the scene during control 36 in both engines, and before that its joints differ by at most 2.2e-16.
  • One-control error across engines (every one of the 1,083 controls started from the original engine's recorded state): tool pose median 1.4e-04, 99th percentile 5.3e-03, maximum 1.4e-02 as exported and median 0, 99th percentile 1.1e-03, maximum 2.3e-03 with the opt-out; robot joints median 6.6e-05, 99th percentile 3.1e-03, maximum 5.9e-03 and median 3.8e-17, 99th percentile 2.3e-03, maximum 4.8e-03.
  • Of these 1,083 single controls, 27 reproduce the original engine's next state to better than 1e-12 (tool pose and robot joints) as exported and 674 with the opt-out; with the opt-out the largest one-control error of the tool pose is 0 while nothing touches the tool (18 controls), 2.5e-04 while only the table or a prop touches it (518 controls), 2.3e-03 while the robot touches it (547 controls).
  • Yardstick inside the original engine (same code, same engine, one start coordinate changed): the x position of the tool at the reset moved by 1e-12 m: 9 of 40 goals in 1,083 controls, tool pose first off by more than 1e-6 at control 95 and by more than 1e-3 at control 115; the angle of arm joint 1 at the reset moved by 1e-12 rad: 9 of 40 goals in 1,083 controls, tool pose first off by more than 1e-6 at control 73 and by more than 1e-3 at control 139.
  • The robot-free scene file against the original model whose robot holds its start posture, with nothing acting on the tool and every control started from the original's recorded state of the tool: the next tool pose agrees to better than 1e-12 in 300 of 300 controls (largest difference 1.4e-17) in MuJoCo 3.3.7 and in 300 of 300 controls (largest difference 8.4e-17) in MuJoCo 3.8.0. Stepped freely over the same 300 controls instead, the two drift apart to at most 1.2e-16 in 3.3.7 and 1.0e-15 in 3.8.0.
  • The two scene files alone across engines, every control started from the tool's state recorded in the original engine: the next tool pose agrees to better than 1e-12 in 0 of 300 controls (largest difference 3.6e-03) as exported and in 300 of 300 controls (largest difference 1.4e-17) with the opt-out.
  • First frame drawn by the original (software renderer) and by ours from the same state: mean difference 1.1 of 255 per pixel, 0.9 % of pixels differ by more than 8. The original's own video ends in the recorded end state.
  • What this means: the reference is an open-loop list of joint targets, and inside the original engine itself a change of 1e-12 in one start coordinate already changes how far it gets. Its outcome is therefore not a stable property of the scene, and a different outcome in MuJoCo 3.8.0 says nothing against the export; the export is judged by the bit-for-bit comparisons above.
  • Not done yet for this task: replacing the original robot (a KUKA iiwa 14 with a left Sharpa hand) by the Tianji + Wuji 2 rig.
  • Our robot in this scene. The arena is the exported robot-free scene file plus exactly these edits: 10 mesh paths made relative to the task folder; the Tianji + Wuji 2 rig attached through one model asset and one attach element inside the frame rig_mount; 3 attributes added to the statistic element so that the model statistics are those of the original model with its own robot. No engine flag is written at this step (the scene file already carries the declared invdiscrete flag) and no collision bit is changed: all 8 colliding scene geoms have bits 1,1, like the 72 collision geoms of the original robot, and collide with our arms (1,1), right hand (2,5) and left hand (4,3) alike. The rig file is neither copied nor edited.
  • Placement. The original robot (a KUKA iiwa 14 with a left Sharpa hand, base at (0, 0.8, 0)) is not kept and the hand that acts is our right one, so the rig is placed by the declared search of the design, with the same rules in all 21 tasks: mount position 0.4 -0.15 -0.30328488575, yaw 270 degrees, right shoulder 0.3 m above the median height of the path. From there our right arm reaches 125 of 125 path samples without an arm link inside scene geometry (98 of 98 hand poses of the original run up to its last goal, 27 of 27 positions of goals the original run did not reach), with a mean distance from joint limits of 0.88 rad. The rig origin lies 0.303 m below the floor plane, which produces no contact and shows in pictures. Seen from the rig, the work area lies 0.57 m from the stand axis, 37 degrees to the right of straight ahead (the design's search has no preference for the direction the rig faces). For information, the same search restricted to mounts that face the work within 45 degrees gives mount position 0.4 -0.15 -0.30328488575, yaw 270 degrees, with 125 of 125 samples reachable and a mean distance from joint limits of 0.88 rad (work area 37 degrees to the right); it is not used.
  • How a left hand is mapped onto our right hand, and two rules this search needed. The pose targets come from the original hand along its recorded run: our knuckle centre is put on the original knuckle centre, our palm normal (the approach direction) along the original palm normal and our fingers along the original fingers; the thumb then lies on the opposite side, since a left hand cannot be superposed on a right one (the flange frames are not used: the knuckles sit 143 mm from the flange in the Sharpa hand and 67 mm in ours). The design's pre-ranking does not separate the candidates here (9,659 of 57,920 have every sample within 0.66 m of the shoulder), so its ties are broken by the design's own preference order measured by inverse kinematics on 8 evenly spaced hand samples; with the tie-break swap.py uses for DexHandExam (distance from the middle of the reach shell) the best of the 20 candidates reaches 1 of those 8. Candidates whose stand or arm bases would stand inside the table or a prop are passed over (4,442 of the 9,659); MuJoCo itself reports no contact between two bodies fixed to the world.
  • S1 passed: 721 compiled scene values are identical in the arena and in the scene file alone (0 differ outside the declared list), the option block and the visual block are identical, and the statistic equals the pinned values of the original model. Against the model the original builder constructs with its own robot (compiled here under MuJoCo 3.8.0), 0 of 721 scene values differ, besides the world body's gravity-compensation value, which no scene file can carry and which applies no force. The rig inside the arena equals the rig compiled alone over 10,016 values, apart from the mount pose of its three root bodies and derived arrays that differ by at most 1.3e-10.
  • S2 passed (gate: rig at rest, its arm motors carrying gravity): stepping the scene with and without our rig from the same state for 1,500 substeps, the scene coordinates differ by at most 1.1e-16 (positions) and 6.7e-14 (velocities), with the same scene contacts on every substep (0 differ), over 3 runs (as is, with scripted pushes on the tool, and without the invdiscrete flag); with a converged solver 3.5e-18. The limits are 1e-12 and 1e-9. For information, the design's first protocol (the rig's motors at zero, so that its arms begin to fall during the substep) gives at most 1.1e-16 and 6.7e-14 over the same runs, which would pass too. Running freely for 2.5 s with the rig held by a servo and touching nothing, the tool's coordinates differ from those in the scene alone by at most 1.9e-16 (the scene alone against itself after a 1e-15 nudge: 1.0e-15).
  • S3 passed: of 496 pairs of a rig collision geom and a scene collision geom, 0 collide differently from the way the scene geom collided with the original robot (read from the builder's model with the iiwa and the Sharpa hand); of 28 scene pairs, 0 changed; no contact exclude joins robot and scene (35 robot-internal excludes in the original, 24 rig-internal ones here).
  • S4 passed: with the scene at the original reset state and our rig at its start posture (the co-simulation's home posture for the right arm (joints 2, 4, 6 = -0.6, -0.8, 0.3), the left arm at the rig's zero posture), 0 robot-to-scene contacts occur in 1,500 substeps (2.5 s; the tool moves 7.7 mm as it settles); at the zero posture the model loads in there are 0; 0 of 8 pairs of a fixed rig part and a fixed scene geom intersect.
  • Reach of our right arm from this mount, by inverse kinematics with our joint limits (no dynamics): of the 98 hand samples (every 5 controls of the original run up to control 483, where it reached its last goal, 13 of 40), 98 are reached by position, 98 by position and approach direction, 98 by position and orientation (5 mm, 5 degrees). Of the 40 goal positions of the task, the knuckle centre of our hand can be brought to 40 (a held tool lay 50 mm from the original knuckle centre in the median). 98 of the 98 hand samples lie outside the 0.36 m inner shell the co-simulation's planners use and 98 within 0.66 m of the shoulder.
  • The goal rule with our rig runs unchanged: the benchmark's tracker (the port's copy that reproduced the original bit for bit) reads the tool's pose only. On the arena, with the tool left alone, it counts 0 of 40 goals (closest approach 118 mm, tolerance 15 mm) and ends the attempt by the 30 s per-goal limit at control 1,800; with the tool set by hand to goal 1, 2 and 3 between controls it counts 1, 2, 3 and moves the green marker each time. The same two tests on the scene without any robot and on the original model with its robot idle give the same counts; over the 1,800 free-running controls with the tool left alone, the distance the rule computes differs from the arena's by at most 3.2e-16 m (no robot) and 2.6e-16 m (original robot), against 4.6e-16 m for the scene without a robot against itself after its tool is moved by 1e-15 m; set to the goals, the tool touches the idle original hand in 1 of 3 controls of the original model, which moves it by up to 9.6 mm.
  • What our hand changes in contact, measured on actual contacts between the tool and a finger: with the original Sharpa hand a hand-to-tool contact has condim 6, sliding friction 1, solref 0.02 1; with our hand condim 4, sliding friction 3, solref 0.004 1, because our hand geoms have priority 1 and MuJoCo then ignores the tool's own values. Tool-to-table contact is untouched. The rig may not be edited, so this is reported, not changed.
  • Our rig alone under this scene's options (implicitfast, elliptic cones, impratio 1, 20 solver iterations, 1.667 ms) against its own options: arm hold drift 2.4e-04 rad against 3.1e-04 rad over 2 s; finger step rise time 50 ms against 52 ms (median of 20 joints), overshoot 6.3 % against 4.7 %; the invdiscrete flag changes the rig by 0 rad (measured once for the suite's single option block, in brush_blue_brush_sweep_forward).
  • What this step did not do: no co-simulation episode, no policy, no attempt; plain MuJoCo 3.8.0 only. The task was built for a left hand and our policy drives the right hand; the reference actions are joint targets of the original robot and cannot be replayed on ours; nothing here shows that our robot can do the task. The light named top follows the centre of mass of the whole model and so stands 94 mm from where it stood in the original at the reset. The binding self-test, tools/check.py and the task folder are other steps, so the status of this task is not changed here.
Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexToolBench · claw hammer · swing_side (MuJoCo) — STANDARD MODE (robot as a service)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **claw hammer** on it.
**Task:** pick up the claw hammer and move it through the demonstrated motion (a sideways hammer swing): bring it to each
of the **40 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `hammer / claw_hammer /
swing_side` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

You control the robot **as if it were real hardware**: the simulator runs in a service you cannot open. You get one
client and **20 resets**: at most 21 episodes, of which the last is graded.

## Rules (real-robot rules)
- **Episodes and resets.** You have **20 resets** (`spec()["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0,
  there is no reset and the one episode is the run). `r.reset()` puts the robot, the tool and the goals back to the same
  starting state and starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended. Within an episode
  nothing is undone: a tool knocked off the table stays there until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: a
  success (every goal reached) ends the run at once, and when your time is up the episode then running is the one
  graded, so do not reset away a good episode late. Resetting does not stop or restore the clock.
- **No privileged state.** You see what the cameras see (RGB, optional depth, with each camera's calibration) plus the
  robot's own joint positions, velocities and targets. No object poses, no success predicate.
- Your only budget is the time limit (`## Time limit`). `meta["time_left_s"]` is the service's count of it, from your first
  request to the service: it never runs out before your time does, so plan by it. There is nothing to hand in: the
  service records every episode, and grades the last one as the trajectory. Leave your script at `/app/output/gen.py` for the
  record.
- Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any published solution for this benchmark; write your own controller.
- Images come back as arrays in a Python object; what you look at and where you store it is up to your code.

## Scoring
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. In this mode goals have **no time limit** (the benchmark gives each goal 10 s). An episode ends when every goal is reached, when your time is up, or after **360,000 control steps (100 min of robot time)**. **Only the last episode is scored.**
**Score: 1 if all 40 goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 40 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.
Full task description (original text, privileged setting; differs from the standard one)
# DexToolBench · claw hammer · swing_side (MuJoCo)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **claw hammer** on it.
**Task:** pick up the claw hammer and move it through the demonstrated motion (a sideways hammer swing): bring it to each
of the **40 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `hammer / claw_hammer /
swing_side` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

## What you hand in
`/app/output/trajectory.npz` — joint position targets, shape `(T, 29)`, one row per control step (1/60 s), each held
for 10 physics steps. Record it with the tooling (below) so the layout is right. The verifier replays it from the
frozen start state in a separate sandbox (MuJoCo on CPU is bit-exact) and scores it. Leave the script that produced it
at `/app/output/gen.py`.

## Scoring (the benchmark's own rule)
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. Each goal has **30 s (1,800 control steps)**; if it is not reached in time the attempt ends there (DexToolBench's own rule is 10 s; relaxed here because your trajectory is replayed offline and you can reset as often as you like). The trajectory may be at most 360,000 control steps.
**Score: 1 if all 40  goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 40 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

## Rules
- The network reaches only the model API and the package registries (PyPI, Debian / Ubuntu archives). Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any
  DexToolBench / SimToolReal solution; write your own controller.
- Only the joint targets count: editing `s.data` (e.g. moving the tool by hand) while debugging changes nothing in
  the replay.

# DexToolBench · mallet hammer · swing_down (MuJoCo) — STANDARD MODE (robot as a service)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **mallet hammer** on it.
**Task:** pick up the mallet hammer and move it through the demonstrated motion (a downward hammer swing): bring it to each
of the **36 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `hammer / mallet_hammer /
swing_down` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

You control the robot **as if it were real hardware**: the simulator runs in a service you cannot open. You get one
client and **20 resets**: at most 21 episodes, of which the last is graded.

## Rules (real-robot rules)
- **Episodes and resets.** You have **20 resets** (`spec()["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0,
  there is no reset and the one episode is the run). `r.reset()` puts the robot, the tool and the goals back to the same
  starting state and starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended. Within an episode
  nothing is undone: a tool knocked off the table stays there until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: a
  success (every goal reached) ends the run at once, and when your time is up the episode then running is the one
  graded, so do not reset away a good episode late. Resetting does not stop or restore the clock.
- **No privileged state.** You see what the cameras see (RGB, optional depth, with each camera's calibration) plus the
  robot's own joint positions, velocities and targets. No object poses, no success predicate.
- Your only budget is the time limit (`## Time limit`). `meta["time_left_s"]` is the service's count of it, from your first
  request to the service: it never runs out before your time does, so plan by it. There is nothing to hand in: the
  service records every episode, and grades the last one as the trajectory. Leave your script at `/app/output/gen.py` for the
  record.
- Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any published solution for this benchmark; write your own controller.
- Images come back as arrays in a Python object; what you look at and where you store it is up to your code.

## Scoring
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. In this mode goals have **no time limit** (the benchmark gives each goal 10 s). An episode ends when every goal is reached, when your time is up, or after **360,000 control steps (100 min of robot time)**. **Only the last episode is scored.**
**Score: 1 if all 36 goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 36 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

# DexToolBench · mallet hammer · swing_down (MuJoCo)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **mallet hammer** on it.
**Task:** pick up the mallet hammer and move it through the demonstrated motion (a downward hammer swing): bring it to each
of the **36 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `hammer / mallet_hammer /
swing_down` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

## What you hand in
`/app/output/trajectory.npz` — joint position targets, shape `(T, 29)`, one row per control step (1/60 s), each held
for 10 physics steps. Record it with the tooling (below) so the layout is right. The verifier replays it from the
frozen start state in a separate sandbox (MuJoCo on CPU is bit-exact) and scores it. Leave the script that produced it
at `/app/output/gen.py`.

## Scoring (the benchmark's own rule)
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. Each goal has **30 s (1,800 control steps)**; if it is not reached in time the attempt ends there (DexToolBench's own rule is 10 s; relaxed here because your trajectory is replayed offline and you can reset as often as you like). The trajectory may be at most 360,000 control steps.
**Score: 1 if all 36  goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 36 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

## Rules
- The network reaches only the model API and the package registries (PyPI, Debian / Ubuntu archives). Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any
  DexToolBench / SimToolReal solution; write your own controller.
- Only the joint targets count: editing `s.data` (e.g. moving the tool by hand) while debugging changes nothing in
  the replay.

The start-state hash e0d1e247200c equals the one recorded in the task, two fresh runs give identical arrays, and the unmodified replay entry point returns the same result (end hash 972638e8cdd8).
  • The scene without the robot is exported as one file written with full precision (the benchmark has no scene file; its scene is built by code). Compiled alone it equals the original model element by element in MuJoCo 3.3.7 (184 arrays identical, 213 belong to kinds of element only the robot has) and in MuJoCo 3.8.0 (194 arrays identical). Different by construction: quantities that count the robot (mass below the world body, camera and light offsets from the model's centre of mass, the automatic statistics), and the world body's gravity-compensation value, which the original sets through its API, no scene file can carry, and which applies no force.
  • The port's own stepping loop and goal rule, run on the original model in MuJoCo 3.3.7, reproduce the original bit for bit: state, goals reached and goal marker after every control and the final hash, over the reference and three altered action sequences (3,307 controls, one of which ends by the per-goal time limit); restarting from each of the 431 recorded states and stepping one control gives exactly zero difference.
  • Under our MuJoCo 3.8.0 the original code needs one guarded line (a flag name that no longer exists). It then gives the recorded start hash and the same reset state, and the port's loop reproduces it bit for bit over 3,093 controls (the reference and the three altered sequences).
  • Both engines compile the same model: 415 of 425 arrays are identical, masses, inertias, geometry and friction included; the 10 others are 9 mesh polygon tables, which the engines build differently, and 1 table of offsets into the file-path buffer (the assets sit at another path on the host). Option entries and flags, read as effective settings, are equal.
  • Outcome of the same reference in our MuJoCo 3.8.0: 0 of 36 goals with the scene as exported, 2 of 36 with MuJoCo's documented opt-out of its newer free-body integration (flag invdiscrete), against 36 of 36 in the original engine.
  • As exported, the two engines compared control by control over 431 controls: after the first control the tool pose differs by 1.4e-04; it first differs by more than 1e-9 at control 1, by more than 1e-6 at control 1 and by more than 1e-3 at control 3. Robot joints first differ by more than 1e-12 at control 28 and by more than 1e-3 at control 28; the robot first touches the scene during control 28 in both engines, and before that its joints differ by at most 2.2e-16.
  • With the opt-out, the two engines compared control by control over 431 controls: after the first control the tool pose differs by 0; it first differs by more than 1e-9 at control 18, by more than 1e-6 at control 18 and by more than 1e-3 at control 25. Robot joints first differ by more than 1e-12 at control 28 and by more than 1e-3 at control 33; the robot first touches the scene during control 28 in both engines, and before that its joints differ by at most 2.2e-16.

  • What this means: inside the original engine a change of 1e-12 in one start coordinate changes the trajectory but not the outcome (36 of 36 goals), so the different outcome in MuJoCo 3.8.0 comes from the engine version. The export itself is judged by the bit-for-bit comparisons above.
  • Not done yet for this task: replacing the original robot (a KUKA iiwa 14 with a left Sharpa hand) by the Tianji + Wuji 2 rig.
  • Our robot in this scene. The arena is the exported robot-free scene file plus exactly these edits: 6 mesh paths made relative to the task folder; the Tianji + Wuji 2 rig attached through one model asset and one attach element inside the frame rig_mount; 3 attributes added to the statistic element so that the model statistics are those of the original model with its own robot. No engine flag is written at this step (the scene file already carries the declared invdiscrete flag) and no collision bit is changed: all 6 colliding scene geoms have bits 1,1, like the 72 collision geoms of the original robot, and collide with our arms (1,1), right hand (2,5) and left hand (4,3) alike. The rig file is neither copied nor edited.
  • Placement. The original robot (a KUKA iiwa 14 with a left Sharpa hand, base at (0, 0.8, 0)) is not kept and the hand that acts is our right one, so the rig is placed by the declared search of the design, with the same rules in all 21 tasks: mount position -0.85 0.9 -0.301620484934, yaw 135 degrees, right shoulder 0.2 m above the median height of the path. From there our right arm reaches 88 of 88 path samples without an arm link inside scene geometry (88 of 88 hand poses of the original run up to its last goal), with a mean distance from joint limits of 0.70 rad. The rig origin lies 0.302 m below the floor plane, which produces no contact and shows in pictures. Seen from the rig, the work area lies 0.44 m from the stand axis, 165 degrees to the right of straight ahead (the design's search has no preference for the direction the rig faces). For information, the same search restricted to mounts that face the work within 45 degrees gives mount position 0.45 -0.15 -0.401620484934, yaw 270 degrees, with 88 of 88 samples reachable and a mean distance from joint limits of 0.67 rad (work area 40 degrees to the right); it is not used.
  • How a left hand is mapped onto our right hand, and two rules this search needed. The pose targets come from the original hand along its recorded run: our knuckle centre is put on the original knuckle centre, our palm normal (the approach direction) along the original palm normal and our fingers along the original fingers; the thumb then lies on the opposite side, since a left hand cannot be superposed on a right one (the flange frames are not used: the knuckles sit 143 mm from the flange in the Sharpa hand and 67 mm in ours). The design's pre-ranking does not separate the candidates here (7,394 of 57,760 have every sample within 0.66 m of the shoulder), so its ties are broken by the design's own preference order measured by inverse kinematics on 8 evenly spaced hand samples; with the tie-break swap.py uses for DexHandExam (distance from the middle of the reach shell) the best of the 20 candidates reaches 8 of those 8. Candidates whose stand or arm bases would stand inside the table or a prop are passed over (4,260 of the 7,394); MuJoCo itself reports no contact between two bodies fixed to the world.
  • S1 passed: 585 compiled scene values are identical in the arena and in the scene file alone (0 differ outside the declared list), the option block and the visual block are identical, and the statistic equals the pinned values of the original model. Against the model the original builder constructs with its own robot (compiled here under MuJoCo 3.8.0), 0 of 585 scene values differ, besides the world body's gravity-compensation value, which no scene file can carry and which applies no force. The rig inside the arena equals the rig compiled alone over 10,016 values, apart from the mount pose of its three root bodies and derived arrays that differ by at most 9.7e-11.
  • S2 passed (gate: rig at rest, its arm motors carrying gravity): stepping the scene with and without our rig from the same state for 1,500 substeps, the scene coordinates differ by at most 1.1e-16 (positions) and 1.1e-14 (velocities), with the same scene contacts on every substep (0 differ), over 3 runs (as is, with scripted pushes on the tool, and without the invdiscrete flag); with a converged solver 5.6e-17. The limits are 1e-12 and 1e-9. For information, the design's first protocol (the rig's motors at zero, so that its arms begin to fall during the substep) gives at most 1.1e-11 and 1.6e-08 over the same runs, which would NOT pass (6 of 4,500 substeps above the limits). Running freely for 2.5 s with the rig held by a servo and touching nothing, the tool's coordinates differ from those in the scene alone by at most 1.6e-12 (the scene alone against itself after a 1e-15 nudge: 1.3e-12).
  • S3 passed: of 372 pairs of a rig collision geom and a scene collision geom, 0 collide differently from the way the scene geom collided with the original robot (read from the builder's model with the iiwa and the Sharpa hand); of 15 scene pairs, 0 changed; no contact exclude joins robot and scene (35 robot-internal excludes in the original, 24 rig-internal ones here).
  • S4 passed: with the scene at the original reset state and our rig at its start posture (the co-simulation's home posture for the right arm (joints 2, 4, 6 = -0.6, -0.8, 0.3), the left arm at the rig's zero posture), 0 robot-to-scene contacts occur in 1,500 substeps (2.5 s; the tool moves 21.0 mm as it settles); at the zero posture the model loads in there are 0; 0 of 8 pairs of a fixed rig part and a fixed scene geom intersect.
  • Reach of our right arm from this mount, by inverse kinematics with our joint limits (no dynamics): of the 88 hand samples (every 5 controls of the original run up to control 431, where it reached its last goal, 36 of 36), 88 are reached by position, 88 by position and approach direction, 88 by position and orientation (5 mm, 5 degrees). Of the 36 goal positions of the task, the knuckle centre of our hand can be brought to 36 (a held tool lay 39 mm from the original knuckle centre in the median). 88 of the 88 hand samples lie outside the 0.36 m inner shell the co-simulation's planners use and 88 within 0.66 m of the shoulder.
  • The goal rule with our rig runs unchanged: the benchmark's tracker (the port's copy that reproduced the original bit for bit) reads the tool's pose only. On the arena, with the tool left alone, it counts 0 of 36 goals (closest approach 114 mm, tolerance 15 mm) and ends the attempt by the 30 s per-goal limit at control 1,800; with the tool set by hand to goal 1, 2 and 3 between controls it counts 1, 2, 3 and moves the green marker each time. The same two tests on the scene without any robot and on the original model with its robot idle give the same counts; over the 1,800 free-running controls with the tool left alone, the distance the rule computes differs from the arena's by at most 1.3e-13 m (no robot) and 2.7e-14 m (original robot), against 1.1e-13 m for the scene without a robot against itself after its tool is moved by 1e-15 m; set to the goals, the tool touches the idle original hand in 1 of 3 controls of the original model, which moves it by up to 2.6 mm.
  • What our hand changes in contact, measured on actual contacts between the tool and a finger: with the original Sharpa hand a hand-to-tool contact has condim 6, sliding friction 1, solref 0.02 1; with our hand condim 4, sliding friction 3, solref 0.004 1, because our hand geoms have priority 1 and MuJoCo then ignores the tool's own values. Tool-to-table contact is untouched. The rig may not be edited, so this is reported, not changed.
  • Our rig alone under this scene's options (implicitfast, elliptic cones, impratio 1, 20 solver iterations, 1.667 ms) against its own options: arm hold drift 2.4e-04 rad against 3.1e-04 rad over 2 s; finger step rise time 50 ms against 52 ms (median of 20 joints), overshoot 6.3 % against 4.7 %; the invdiscrete flag changes the rig by 0 rad (measured once for the suite's single option block, in brush_blue_brush_sweep_forward).
  • What this step did not do: no co-simulation episode, no policy, no attempt; plain MuJoCo 3.8.0 only. The task was built for a left hand and our policy drives the right hand; the reference actions are joint targets of the original robot and cannot be replayed on ours; nothing here shows that our robot can do the task. The light named top follows the centre of mass of the whole model and so stands 119 mm from where it stood in the original at the reset. The binding self-test, tools/check.py and the task folder are other steps, so the status of this task is not changed here.

# DexToolBench · sharpie marker · draw_smile (MuJoCo) — STANDARD MODE (robot as a service)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **sharpie marker** on it.
**Task:** pick up the sharpie marker and move it through the demonstrated motion (drawing a smiley face): bring it to each
of the **36 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `marker / sharpie_marker /
draw_smile` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

You control the robot **as if it were real hardware**: the simulator runs in a service you cannot open. You get one
client and **20 resets**: at most 21 episodes, of which the last is graded.

## Rules (real-robot rules)
- **Episodes and resets.** You have **20 resets** (`spec()["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0,
  there is no reset and the one episode is the run). `r.reset()` puts the robot, the tool and the goals back to the same
  starting state and starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended. Within an episode
  nothing is undone: a tool knocked off the table stays there until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: a
  success (every goal reached) ends the run at once, and when your time is up the episode then running is the one
  graded, so do not reset away a good episode late. Resetting does not stop or restore the clock.
- **No privileged state.** You see what the cameras see (RGB, optional depth, with each camera's calibration) plus the
  robot's own joint positions, velocities and targets. No object poses, no success predicate.
- Your only budget is the time limit (`## Time limit`). `meta["time_left_s"]` is the service's count of it, from your first
  request to the service: it never runs out before your time does, so plan by it. There is nothing to hand in: the
  service records every episode, and grades the last one as the trajectory. Leave your script at `/app/output/gen.py` for the
  record.
- Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any published solution for this benchmark; write your own controller.
- Images come back as arrays in a Python object; what you look at and where you store it is up to your code.

## Scoring
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. In this mode goals have **no time limit** (the benchmark gives each goal 10 s). An episode ends when every goal is reached, when your time is up, or after **360,000 control steps (100 min of robot time)**. **Only the last episode is scored.**
**Score: 1 if all 36 goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 36 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

# DexToolBench · sharpie marker · draw_smile (MuJoCo)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **sharpie marker** on it.
**Task:** pick up the sharpie marker and move it through the demonstrated motion (drawing a smiley face): bring it to each
of the **36 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `marker / sharpie_marker /
draw_smile` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

## What you hand in
`/app/output/trajectory.npz` — joint position targets, shape `(T, 29)`, one row per control step (1/60 s), each held
for 10 physics steps. Record it with the tooling (below) so the layout is right. The verifier replays it from the
frozen start state in a separate sandbox (MuJoCo on CPU is bit-exact) and scores it. Leave the script that produced it
at `/app/output/gen.py`.

## Scoring (the benchmark's own rule)
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. Each goal has **30 s (1,800 control steps)**; if it is not reached in time the attempt ends there (DexToolBench's own rule is 10 s; relaxed here because your trajectory is replayed offline and you can reset as often as you like). The trajectory may be at most 360,000 control steps.
**Score: 1 if all 36  goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 36 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

## Rules
- The network reaches only the model API and the package registries (PyPI, Debian / Ubuntu archives). Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any
  DexToolBench / SimToolReal solution; write your own controller.
- Only the joint targets count: editing `s.data` (e.g. moving the tool by hand) while debugging changes nothing in
  the replay.

For information, the design's first protocol (the rig's motors at zero, so that its arms begin to fall during the substep) gives at most 3.0e-11 and 4.2e-08 over the same runs, which would NOT pass (7 of 4,500 substeps above the limits). Running freely for 2.5 s with the rig held by a servo and touching nothing, the tool's coordinates differ from those in the scene alone by at most 6.3e-03 (the scene alone against itself after a 1e-15 nudge: 6.2e-03).
  • S3 passed: of 372 pairs of a rig collision geom and a scene collision geom, 0 collide differently from the way the scene geom collided with the original robot (read from the builder's model with the iiwa and the Sharpa hand); of 15 scene pairs, 0 changed; no contact exclude joins robot and scene (35 robot-internal excludes in the original, 24 rig-internal ones here).

  • Reach of our right arm from this mount, by inverse kinematics with our joint limits (no dynamics): of the 110 hand samples (every 5 controls of the original run up to control 544, where it reached its last goal, 25 of 25), 110 are reached by position, 110 by position and approach direction, 110 by position and orientation (5 mm, 5 degrees). Of the 25 goal positions of the task, the knuckle centre of our hand can be brought to 25 (a held tool lay 34 mm from the original knuckle centre in the median). 110 of the 110 hand samples lie outside the 0.36 m inner shell the co-simulation's planners use and 110 within 0.66 m of the shoulder.

# DexToolBench · sharpie marker · write_c (MuJoCo) — STANDARD MODE (robot as a service)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **sharpie marker** on it.
**Task:** pick up the sharpie marker and move it through the demonstrated motion (writing the letter C): bring it to each
of the **25 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `marker / sharpie_marker /
write_c` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

You control the robot **as if it were real hardware**: the simulator runs in a service you cannot open. You get one
client and **20 resets**: at most 21 episodes, of which the last is graded.

## Rules (real-robot rules)
- **Episodes and resets.** You have **20 resets** (`spec()["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0,
  there is no reset and the one episode is the run). `r.reset()` puts the robot, the tool and the goals back to the same
  starting state and starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended. Within an episode
  nothing is undone: a tool knocked off the table stays there until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: a
  success (every goal reached) ends the run at once, and when your time is up the episode then running is the one
  graded, so do not reset away a good episode late. Resetting does not stop or restore the clock.
- **No privileged state.** You see what the cameras see (RGB, optional depth, with each camera's calibration) plus the
  robot's own joint positions, velocities and targets. No object poses, no success predicate.
- Your only budget is the time limit (`## Time limit`). `meta["time_left_s"]` is the service's count of it, from your first
  request to the service: it never runs out before your time does, so plan by it. There is nothing to hand in: the
  service records every episode, and grades the last one as the trajectory. Leave your script at `/app/output/gen.py` for the
  record.
- Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any published solution for this benchmark; write your own controller.
- Images come back as arrays in a Python object; what you look at and where you store it is up to your code.

## Scoring
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. In this mode goals have **no time limit** (the benchmark gives each goal 10 s). An episode ends when every goal is reached, when your time is up, or after **360,000 control steps (100 min of robot time)**. **Only the last episode is scored.**
**Score: 1 if all 25 goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 25 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

# DexToolBench · sharpie marker · write_c (MuJoCo)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **sharpie marker** on it.
**Task:** pick up the sharpie marker and move it through the demonstrated motion (writing the letter C): bring it to each
of the **25 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `marker / sharpie_marker /
write_c` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

## What you hand in
`/app/output/trajectory.npz` — joint position targets, shape `(T, 29)`, one row per control step (1/60 s), each held
for 10 physics steps. Record it with the tooling (below) so the layout is right. The verifier replays it from the
frozen start state in a separate sandbox (MuJoCo on CPU is bit-exact) and scores it. Leave the script that produced it
at `/app/output/gen.py`.

## Scoring (the benchmark's own rule)
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. Each goal has **30 s (1,800 control steps)**; if it is not reached in time the attempt ends there (DexToolBench's own rule is 10 s; relaxed here because your trajectory is replayed offline and you can reset as often as you like). The trajectory may be at most 360,000 control steps.
**Score: 1 if all 25  goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 25 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

## Rules
- The network reaches only the model API and the package registries (PyPI, Debian / Ubuntu archives). Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any
  DexToolBench / SimToolReal solution; write your own controller.
- Only the joint targets count: editing `s.data` (e.g. moving the tool by hand) while debugging changes nothing in
  the replay.

  • Original environment (the benchmark's own code, MuJoCo 3.3.7, run here in its pinned Docker image): the reference reaches 19 of 29 goals; its 1,057 action rows end there, the result the task's README documents. The start-state hash 592c57bb52ad equals the one recorded in the task, two fresh runs give identical arrays, and the unmodified replay entry point returns the same result (end hash e621ae66727b).
  • The scene without the robot is exported as one file written with full precision (the benchmark has no scene file; its scene is built by code). Compiled alone it equals the original model element by element in MuJoCo 3.3.7 (184 arrays identical, 213 belong to kinds of element only the robot has) and in MuJoCo 3.8.0 (194 arrays identical). Different by construction: quantities that count the robot (mass below the world body, camera and light offsets from the model's centre of mass, the automatic statistics), and the world body's gravity-compensation value, which the original sets through its API, no scene file can carry, and which applies no force.
  • The port's own stepping loop and goal rule, run on the original model in MuJoCo 3.3.7, reproduce the original bit for bit: state, goals reached and goal marker after every control and the final hash, over the reference and three altered action sequences (5,428 controls, one of which ends by the per-goal time limit); restarting from each of the 1,057 recorded states and stepping one control gives exactly zero difference.
  • Under our MuJoCo 3.8.0 the original code needs one guarded line (a flag name that no longer exists). It then gives the recorded start hash and the same reset state, and the port's loop reproduces it bit for bit over 5,108 controls (the reference and the three altered sequences).
  • Both engines compile the same model: 415 of 425 arrays are identical, masses, inertias, geometry and friction included; the 10 others are 9 mesh polygon tables, which the engines build differently, and 1 table of offsets into the file-path buffer (the assets sit at another path on the host). Option entries and flags, read as effective settings, are equal.
  • Outcome of the same reference in our MuJoCo 3.8.0: 2 of 29 goals with the scene as exported, 19 of 29 with MuJoCo's documented opt-out of its newer free-body integration (flag invdiscrete), against 19 of 29 in the original engine.
  • As exported, the two engines compared control by control over 1,057 controls: after the first control the tool pose differs by 1.4e-04; it first differs by more than 1e-9 at control 1, by more than 1e-6 at control 1 and by more than 1e-3 at control 3. Robot joints first differ by more than 1e-12 at control 32 and by more than 1e-3 at control 32; the robot first touches the scene during control 28 in both engines, and before that its joints differ by at most 8.9e-16.
  • With the opt-out, the two engines compared control by control over 1,057 controls: after the first control the tool pose differs by 0; it first differs by more than 1e-9 at control 5, by more than 1e-6 at control 5 and by more than 1e-3 at control 6. Robot joints first differ by more than 1e-12 at control 32 and by more than 1e-3 at control 34; the robot first touches the scene during control 28 in both engines, and before that its joints differ by at most 8.9e-16.
  • One-control error across engines (every one of the 1,057 controls started from the original engine's recorded state): tool pose median 2.4e-04, 99th percentile 6.9e-03, maximum 2.6e-02 as exported and median 2.6e-05, 99th percentile 3.9e-03, maximum 1.8e-02 with the opt-out; robot joints median 1.7e-04, 99th percentile 4.2e-03, maximum 1.2e-02 and median 8.4e-06, 99th percentile 4.0e-03, maximum 1.2e-02.
  • Of these 1,057 single controls, 0 reproduce the original engine's next state to better than 1e-12 (tool pose and robot joints) as exported and 363 with the opt-out; with the opt-out the largest one-control error of the tool pose is 0 while nothing touches the tool (9 controls), 6.9e-03 while only the table or a prop touches it (115 controls), 1.8e-02 while the robot touches it (933 controls).
  • Yardstick inside the original engine (same code, same engine, one start coordinate changed): the x position of the tool at the reset moved by 1e-12 m: 20 of 29 goals in 1,057 controls, tool pose first off by more than 1e-6 at control 148 and by more than 1e-3 at control 193; the angle of arm joint 1 at the reset moved by 1e-12 rad: 19 of 29 goals in 1,057 controls, tool pose first off by more than 1e-6 at control 175 and by more than 1e-3 at control 198.
  • The robot-free scene file against the original model whose robot holds its start posture, with nothing acting on the tool and every control started from the original's recorded state of the tool: the next tool pose agrees to better than 1e-12 in 300 of 300 controls (largest difference 1.1e-16) in MuJoCo 3.3.7 and in 298 of 300 controls (largest difference 9.9e-05) in MuJoCo 3.8.0. Stepped freely over the same 300 controls instead, the two drift apart to at most 1.5e-01 in 3.3.7 and 1.0e-01 in 3.8.0.
  • The two scene files alone across engines, every control started from the tool's state recorded in the original engine: the next tool pose agrees to better than 1e-12 in 0 of 300 controls (largest difference 6.3e-03) as exported and in 11 of 300 controls (largest difference 6.1e-03) with the opt-out.
  • First frame drawn by the original (software renderer) and by ours from the same state: mean difference 0.9 of 255 per pixel, 0.6 % of pixels differ by more than 8. The original's own video ends in the recorded end state.
  • What this means: the reference is an open-loop list of joint targets, and inside the original engine itself a change of 1e-12 in one start coordinate already changes how far it gets. Its outcome is therefore not a stable property of the scene, and a different outcome in MuJoCo 3.8.0 says nothing against the export; the export is judged by the bit-for-bit comparisons above.
  • Not done yet for this task: replacing the original robot (a KUKA iiwa 14 with a left Sharpa hand) by the Tianji + Wuji 2 rig.
  • Our robot in this scene. The arena is the exported robot-free scene file plus exactly these edits: 6 mesh paths made relative to the task folder; the Tianji + Wuji 2 rig attached through one model asset and one attach element inside the frame rig_mount; 3 attributes added to the statistic element so that the model statistics are those of the original model with its own robot. No engine flag is written at this step (the scene file already carries the declared invdiscrete flag) and no collision bit is changed: all 6 colliding scene geoms have bits 1,1, like the 72 collision geoms of the original robot, and collide with our arms (1,1), right hand (2,5) and left hand (4,3) alike. The rig file is neither copied nor edited.
  • Placement. The original robot (a KUKA iiwa 14 with a left Sharpa hand, base at (0, 0.8, 0)) is not kept and the hand that acts is our right one, so the rig is placed by the declared search of the design, with the same rules in all 21 tasks: mount position 0.5 -0.15 -0.503026479445, yaw 270 degrees, right shoulder 0.1 m above the median height of the path. From there our right arm reaches 103 of 103 path samples without an arm link inside scene geometry (93 of 93 hand poses of the original run up to its last goal, 10 of 10 positions of goals the original run did not reach), with a mean distance from joint limits of 0.88 rad. The rig origin lies 0.503 m below the floor plane, which produces no contact and shows in pictures. Seen from the rig, the work area lies 0.63 m from the stand axis, 37 degrees to the right of straight ahead (the design's search has no preference for the direction the rig faces). For information, the same search restricted to mounts that face the work within 45 degrees gives mount position 0.5 -0.15 -0.503026479445, yaw 270 degrees, with 103 of 103 samples reachable and a mean distance from joint limits of 0.88 rad (work area 37 degrees to the right); it is not used.
  • How a left hand is mapped onto our right hand, and two rules this search needed. The pose targets come from the original hand along its recorded run: our knuckle centre is put on the original knuckle centre, our palm normal (the approach direction) along the original palm normal and our fingers along the original fingers; the thumb then lies on the opposite side, since a left hand cannot be superposed on a right one (the flange frames are not used: the knuckles sit 143 mm from the flange in the Sharpa hand and 67 mm in ours). The design's pre-ranking does not separate the candidates here (9,107 of 57,984 have every sample within 0.66 m of the shoulder), so its ties are broken by the design's own preference order measured by inverse kinematics on 8 evenly spaced hand samples; with the tie-break swap.py uses for DexHandExam (distance from the middle of the reach shell) the best of the 20 candidates reaches 8 of those 8. Candidates whose stand or arm bases would stand inside the table or a prop are passed over (4,703 of the 9,107); MuJoCo itself reports no contact between two bodies fixed to the world.
  • S1 passed: 585 compiled scene values are identical in the arena and in the scene file alone (0 differ outside the declared list), the option block and the visual block are identical, and the statistic equals the pinned values of the original model. Against the model the original builder constructs with its own robot (compiled here under MuJoCo 3.8.0), 0 of 585 scene values differ, besides the world body's gravity-compensation value, which no scene file can carry and which applies no force. The rig inside the arena equals the rig compiled alone over 10,016 values, apart from the mount pose of its three root bodies and derived arrays that differ by at most 1.6e-10.
  • S2 passed (gate: rig at rest, its arm motors carrying gravity): stepping the scene with and without our rig from the same state for 1,500 substeps, the scene coordinates differ by at most 1.1e-16 (positions) and 1.1e-13 (velocities), with the same scene contacts on every substep (0 differ), over 3 runs (as is, with scripted pushes on the tool, and without the invdiscrete flag); with a converged solver 1.1e-16. The limits are 1e-12 and 1e-9. For information, the design's first protocol (the rig's motors at zero, so that its arms begin to fall during the substep) gives at most 6.2e-11 and 8.5e-08 over the same runs, which would NOT pass (108 of 4,500 substeps above the limits). Running freely for 2.5 s with the rig held by a servo and touching nothing, the tool's coordinates differ from those in the scene alone by at most 1.5e-01 (the scene alone against itself after a 1e-15 nudge: 1.5e-01).
  • S3 passed: of 372 pairs of a rig collision geom and a scene collision geom, 0 collide differently from the way the scene geom collided with the original robot (read from the builder's model with the iiwa and the Sharpa hand); of 15 scene pairs, 0 changed; no contact exclude joins robot and scene (35 robot-internal excludes in the original, 24 rig-internal ones here).
  • S4 passed: with the scene at the original reset state and our rig at its start posture (the co-simulation's home posture for the right arm (joints 2, 4, 6 = -0.6, -0.8, 0.3), the left arm at the rig's zero posture), 0 robot-to-scene contacts occur in 1,500 substeps (2.5 s; the tool moves 14.1 mm as it settles); at the zero posture the model loads in there are 0; 0 of 8 pairs of a fixed rig part and a fixed scene geom intersect.
  • Reach of our right arm from this mount, by inverse kinematics with our joint limits (no dynamics): of the 93 hand samples (every 5 controls of the original run up to control 457, where it reached its last goal, 19 of 29), 93 are reached by position, 93 by position and approach direction, 93 by position and orientation (5 mm, 5 degrees). Of the 29 goal positions of the task, the knuckle centre of our hand can be brought to 29 (a held tool lay 47 mm from the original knuckle centre in the median). 93 of the 93 hand samples lie outside the 0.36 m inner shell the co-simulation's planners use and 93 within 0.66 m of the shoulder.
  • The goal rule with our rig runs unchanged: the benchmark's tracker (the port's copy that reproduced the original bit for bit) reads the tool's pose only. On the arena, with the tool left alone, it counts 0 of 29 goals (closest approach 113 mm, tolerance 15 mm) and ends the attempt by the 30 s per-goal limit at control 1,800; with the tool set by hand to goal 1, 2 and 3 between controls it counts 1, 2, 3 and moves the green marker each time. The same two tests on the scene without any robot and on the original model with its robot idle give the same counts; over the 1,800 free-running controls with the tool left alone, the distance the rule computes differs from the arena's by at most 1.2e-02 m (no robot) and 1.2e-02 m (original robot), against 1.1e-02 m for the scene without a robot against itself after its tool is moved by 1e-15 m; set to the goals, the tool touches the idle original hand in 2 of 3 controls of the original model, which moves it by up to 6.4 mm.
  • What our hand changes in contact, measured on actual contacts between the tool and a finger: with the original Sharpa hand a hand-to-tool contact has condim 6, sliding friction 1, solref 0.02 1; with our hand condim 4, sliding friction 3, solref 0.004 1, because our hand geoms have priority 1 and MuJoCo then ignores the tool's own values. Tool-to-table contact is untouched. The rig may not be edited, so this is reported, not changed.
  • Our rig alone under this scene's options (implicitfast, elliptic cones, impratio 1, 20 solver iterations, 1.667 ms) against its own options: arm hold drift 2.4e-04 rad against 3.1e-04 rad over 2 s; finger step rise time 50 ms against 52 ms (median of 20 joints), overshoot 6.3 % against 4.7 %; the invdiscrete flag changes the rig by 0 rad (measured once for the suite's single option block, in brush_blue_brush_sweep_forward).
  • What this step did not do: no co-simulation episode, no policy, no attempt; plain MuJoCo 3.8.0 only. The task was built for a left hand and our policy drives the right hand; the reference actions are joint targets of the original robot and cannot be replayed on ours; nothing here shows that our robot can do the task. The light named top follows the centre of mass of the whole model and so stands 91 mm from where it stood in the original at the reset. The binding self-test, tools/check.py and the task folder are other steps, so the status of this task is not changed here.
Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexToolBench · staples marker · write_c (MuJoCo) — STANDARD MODE (robot as a service)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **staples marker** on it.
**Task:** pick up the staples marker and move it through the demonstrated motion (writing the letter C): bring it to each
of the **29 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `marker / staples_marker /
write_c` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

You control the robot **as if it were real hardware**: the simulator runs in a service you cannot open. You get one
client and **20 resets**: at most 21 episodes, of which the last is graded.

## Rules (real-robot rules)
- **Episodes and resets.** You have **20 resets** (`spec()["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0,
  there is no reset and the one episode is the run). `r.reset()` puts the robot, the tool and the goals back to the same
  starting state and starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended. Within an episode
  nothing is undone: a tool knocked off the table stays there until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: a
  success (every goal reached) ends the run at once, and when your time is up the episode then running is the one
  graded, so do not reset away a good episode late. Resetting does not stop or restore the clock.
- **No privileged state.** You see what the cameras see (RGB, optional depth, with each camera's calibration) plus the
  robot's own joint positions, velocities and targets. No object poses, no success predicate.
- Your only budget is the time limit (`## Time limit`). `meta["time_left_s"]` is the service's count of it, from your first
  request to the service: it never runs out before your time does, so plan by it. There is nothing to hand in: the
  service records every episode, and grades the last one as the trajectory. Leave your script at `/app/output/gen.py` for the
  record.
- Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any published solution for this benchmark; write your own controller.
- Images come back as arrays in a Python object; what you look at and where you store it is up to your code.

## Scoring
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. In this mode goals have **no time limit** (the benchmark gives each goal 10 s). An episode ends when every goal is reached, when your time is up, or after **360,000 control steps (100 min of robot time)**. **Only the last episode is scored.**
**Score: 1 if all 29 goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 29 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.
Full task description (original text, privileged setting; differs from the standard one)
# DexToolBench · staples marker · write_c (MuJoCo)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **staples marker** on it.
**Task:** pick up the staples marker and move it through the demonstrated motion (writing the letter C): bring it to each
of the **29 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `marker / staples_marker /
write_c` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

## What you hand in
`/app/output/trajectory.npz` — joint position targets, shape `(T, 29)`, one row per control step (1/60 s), each held
for 10 physics steps. Record it with the tooling (below) so the layout is right. The verifier replays it from the
frozen start state in a separate sandbox (MuJoCo on CPU is bit-exact) and scores it. Leave the script that produced it
at `/app/output/gen.py`.

## Scoring (the benchmark's own rule)
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. Each goal has **30 s (1,800 control steps)**; if it is not reached in time the attempt ends there (DexToolBench's own rule is 10 s; relaxed here because your trajectory is replayed offline and you can reset as often as you like). The trajectory may be at most 360,000 control steps.
**Score: 1 if all 29  goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 29 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

## Rules
- The network reaches only the model API and the package registries (PyPI, Debian / Ubuntu archives). Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any
  DexToolBench / SimToolReal solution; write your own controller.
- Only the joint targets count: editing `s.data` (e.g. moving the tool by hand) while debugging changes nothing in
  the replay.

# DexToolBench · long screwdriver · spin_horizontal (MuJoCo) — STANDARD MODE (robot as a service)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **long screwdriver** on it.
**Task:** pick up the long screwdriver and move it through the demonstrated motion (spinning it about a horizontal axis): bring it to each
of the **31 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `screwdriver / long_screwdriver /
spin_horizontal` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

You control the robot **as if it were real hardware**: the simulator runs in a service you cannot open. You get one
client and **20 resets**: at most 21 episodes, of which the last is graded.

## Rules (real-robot rules)
- **Episodes and resets.** You have **20 resets** (`spec()["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0,
  there is no reset and the one episode is the run). `r.reset()` puts the robot, the tool and the goals back to the same
  starting state and starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended. Within an episode
  nothing is undone: a tool knocked off the table stays there until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: a
  success (every goal reached) ends the run at once, and when your time is up the episode then running is the one
  graded, so do not reset away a good episode late. Resetting does not stop or restore the clock.
- **No privileged state.** You see what the cameras see (RGB, optional depth, with each camera's calibration) plus the
  robot's own joint positions, velocities and targets. No object poses, no success predicate.
- Your only budget is the time limit (`## Time limit`). `meta["time_left_s"]` is the service's count of it, from your first
  request to the service: it never runs out before your time does, so plan by it. There is nothing to hand in: the
  service records every episode, and grades the last one as the trajectory. Leave your script at `/app/output/gen.py` for the
  record.
- Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any published solution for this benchmark; write your own controller.
- Images come back as arrays in a Python object; what you look at and where you store it is up to your code.

## Scoring
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. In this mode goals have **no time limit** (the benchmark gives each goal 10 s). An episode ends when every goal is reached, when your time is up, or after **360,000 control steps (100 min of robot time)**. **Only the last episode is scored.**
**Score: 1 if all 31 goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 31 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

# DexToolBench · long screwdriver · spin_horizontal (MuJoCo)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **long screwdriver** on it.
**Task:** pick up the long screwdriver and move it through the demonstrated motion (spinning it about a horizontal axis): bring it to each
of the **31 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `screwdriver / long_screwdriver /
spin_horizontal` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

## What you hand in
`/app/output/trajectory.npz` — joint position targets, shape `(T, 29)`, one row per control step (1/60 s), each held
for 10 physics steps. Record it with the tooling (below) so the layout is right. The verifier replays it from the
frozen start state in a separate sandbox (MuJoCo on CPU is bit-exact) and scores it. Leave the script that produced it
at `/app/output/gen.py`.

## Scoring (the benchmark's own rule)
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. Each goal has **30 s (1,800 control steps)**; if it is not reached in time the attempt ends there (DexToolBench's own rule is 10 s; relaxed here because your trajectory is replayed offline and you can reset as often as you like). The trajectory may be at most 360,000 control steps.
**Score: 1 if all 31  goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 31 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

## Rules
- The network reaches only the model API and the package registries (PyPI, Debian / Ubuntu archives). Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any
  DexToolBench / SimToolReal solution; write your own controller.
- Only the joint targets count: editing `s.data` (e.g. moving the tool by hand) while debugging changes nothing in
  the replay.

Full task description (original text, standard setting)
# DexToolBench · short screwdriver · spin_horizontal (MuJoCo) — STANDARD MODE (robot as a service)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **short screwdriver** on it.
**Task:** pick up the short screwdriver and move it through the demonstrated motion (spinning it about a horizontal axis): bring it to each
of the **38 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `screwdriver / short_screwdriver /
spin_horizontal` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

You control the robot **as if it were real hardware**: the simulator runs in a service you cannot open. You get one
client and **20 resets**: at most 21 episodes, of which the last is graded.

## Rules (real-robot rules)
- **Episodes and resets.** You have **20 resets** (`spec()["budget"]["reset"]`, which is authoritative: if it says 0,
  there is no reset and the one episode is the run). `r.reset()` puts the robot, the tool and the goals back to the same
  starting state and starts a new episode, either abandoning the running one or after one has ended. Within an episode
  nothing is undone: a tool knocked off the table stays there until you reset. **Only the last episode is graded**: a
  success (every goal reached) ends the run at once, and when your time is up the episode then running is the one
  graded, so do not reset away a good episode late. Resetting does not stop or restore the clock.
- **No privileged state.** You see what the cameras see (RGB, optional depth, with each camera's calibration) plus the
  robot's own joint positions, velocities and targets. No object poses, no success predicate.
- Your only budget is the time limit (`## Time limit`). `meta["time_left_s"]` is the service's count of it, from your first
  request to the service: it never runs out before your time does, so plan by it. There is nothing to hand in: the
  service records every episode, and grades the last one as the trajectory. Leave your script at `/app/output/gen.py` for the
  record.
- Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any published solution for this benchmark; write your own controller.
- Images come back as arrays in a Python object; what you look at and where you store it is up to your code.

## Scoring
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. In this mode goals have **no time limit** (the benchmark gives each goal 10 s). An episode ends when every goal is reached, when your time is up, or after **360,000 control steps (100 min of robot time)**. **Only the last episode is scored.**
**Score: 1 if all 38 goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 38 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.
Full task description (original text, privileged setting; differs from the standard one)
# DexToolBench · short screwdriver · spin_horizontal (MuJoCo)

A KUKA iiwa 14 arm with a 22-joint **Sharpa HA4** dexterous hand stands next to a table with a **short screwdriver** on it.
**Task:** pick up the short screwdriver and move it through the demonstrated motion (spinning it about a horizontal axis): bring it to each
of the **38 goal poses in order** (the green ghost tool shows the current goal). This is task `screwdriver / short_screwdriver /
spin_horizontal` of DexToolBench (SimToolReal), run here in plain MuJoCo.

## What you hand in
`/app/output/trajectory.npz` — joint position targets, shape `(T, 29)`, one row per control step (1/60 s), each held
for 10 physics steps. Record it with the tooling (below) so the layout is right. The verifier replays it from the
frozen start state in a separate sandbox (MuJoCo on CPU is bit-exact) and scores it. Leave the script that produced it
at `/app/output/gen.py`.

## Scoring (the benchmark's own rule)
The current goal counts as reached when all 8 corners of the tool's grasp box (0.141 × 0.030 × 0.027 m, scaled by
1.5, in the tool's frame) are within **1.5 cm** of the same corners at the goal pose; then the next goal becomes
current. Each goal has **30 s (1,800 control steps)**; if it is not reached in time the attempt ends there (DexToolBench's own rule is 10 s; relaxed here because your trajectory is replayed offline and you can reset as often as you like). The trajectory may be at most 360,000 control steps.
**Score: 1 if all 38  goals are reached, else 0.** Goals reached / 38 is reported as `progress`; there is no partial credit.

## Rules
- The network reaches only the model API and the package registries (PyPI, Debian / Ubuntu archives). Do not use pretrained manipulation policies or any
  DexToolBench / SimToolReal solution; write your own controller.
- Only the joint targets count: editing `s.data` (e.g. moving the tool by hand) while debugging changes nothing in
  the replay.
